In many cases, the superiority of probes is simply attributable to better calibration on uncertain answers rather than a greater fraction of correct, high-confidence answers. In some cases, queries and probes perform better on different subsets of inputs, and accuracy can further be improved by ensembling the two. Code is available at github.com/lingo-mit/lm-truthfulness.

papers.title: The Language Model Understood the Prompt was Ambiguous: Probing\n Syntactic Uncertainty Through Generation
papers.research_question: To what extent do neural language models exhibit uncertainty over syntactic analyses when processing temporarily ambiguous inputs, and how is that uncertainty modulated by disambiguating cues?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to probe syntactic uncertainty in language models by generating completions and estimating the probability of each interpretation based on the distribution of parses. It finds that LMs can track multiple analyses simultaneously and are sensitive to disambiguating cues, though with some limitations.
papers.conclusion: Generating completions is an informative tool for probing a language model's syntactic uncertainty, revealing that LMs track multiple analyses and adapt to disambiguating cues, though challenges remain in automatic classification and some disambiguation failures.
papers.key_findings:
Language models exhibit syntactic uncertainty when processing temporary ambiguities, often considering multiple analyses in parallel.
The degree of bias towards one analysis varies across ambiguity types and specific sentences.
Models are generally sensitive to disambiguating cues and shift uncertainty appropriately, but exhibit issues with NP/Z and Noun/Verb ambiguities.
Decoding strategies (like nucleus sampling or temperature) that focus on high-probability words increase the bias towards the preferred interpretation.
The generation-based method aligns with surprisal-based analysis but provides additional insights, such as revealing ungrammatical blended continuations.
papers.limitation: Reliance on automatic classification (a syntactic parser) introduces noise and cannot detect ungrammatical or unclear completions.
future_direction: Determine if inter-item variation in model preferences mirrors human expectations and/or corpus statistics.
Overcome limitations of the method, such as improving classification and detecting ungrammatical completions.
papers.abstract:
Temporary syntactic ambiguities arise when the beginning of a sentence is
compatible with multiple syntactic analyses. We inspect to which extent neural
language models (LMs) exhibit uncertainty over such analyses when processing
temporarily ambiguous inputs, and how that uncertainty is modulated by
disambiguating cues. We probe the LM's expectations by generating from it: we
use stochastic decoding to derive a set of sentence completions, and estimate
the probability that the LM assigns to each interpretation based on the
distribution of parses across completions. Unlike scoring-based methods for
targeted syntactic evaluation, this technique makes it possible to explore
completions that are not hypothesized in advance by the researcher. We apply
this method to study the behavior of two LMs (GPT2 and an LSTM) on three types
of temporary ambiguity, using materials from human sentence processing
experiments. We find that LMs can track multiple analyses simultaneously; the
degree of uncertainty varies across constructions and contexts. As a response
to disambiguating cues, the LMs often select the correct interpretation, but
occasional errors point to potential areas of improvement.

papers.title: Feature Hedging: Correlated Features Break Narrow Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Why do sparse autoencoders (SAEs) underperform relative to other techniques, and can we fix the problems? Specifically, the paper investigates the problem of 'feature hedging' in narrow SAEs.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies 'feature hedging' as a fundamental problem in narrow sparse autoencoders (SAEs) where correlated features are merged, degrading monosemanticity, and proposes an improved variant called balance matryoshka SAEs to mitigate this issue.
papers.conclusion: Feature hedging is a core theoretical problem in SAEs that contributes to their underperformance, and the proposed balance matryoshka SAE architecture is a step towards addressing both hedging and absorption, though both problems remain.
papers.key_findings:
Feature hedging occurs when an SAE is too narrow to represent all underlying features and features are correlated, causing the SAE to merge components of correlated features into single latents.
Hedging is caused by the reconstruction (MSE) loss and becomes more severe the narrower the SAE.
In LLM SAEs, hedging is likely the norm due to the high number of correlated features and the SAE being narrower than the number of underlying features.
Balance matryoshka SAEs, which tune the relative loss coefficients between inner and outer levels, can improve performance by better balancing the competing forces of hedging and absorption.
SAE width is not a neutral hyperparameter: narrower SAEs suffer more from hedging, while wider SAEs suffer more from absorption.
papers.limitation: Only test hedging in SAEs up to 65k latents on LLMs with 2b parameters due to compute constraints.
future_direction: Improving balance matryoshka SAEs by learning different balancing coefficients per latent rather than a single coefficient for all latents.
papers.abstract: It is assumed that sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose polysemantic activations into interpretable linear directions, as long as the activations are composed of sparse linear combinations of underlying features. However, we find that if an SAE is more narrow than the number of underlying "true features" on which it is trained, and there is correlation between features, the SAE will merge components of correlated features together, thus destroying monosemanticity. In LLM SAEs, these two conditions are almost certainly true. This phenomenon, which we call feature hedging, is caused by SAE reconstruction loss, and is more severe the narrower the SAE. In this work, we introduce the problem of feature hedging and study it both theoretically in toy models and empirically in SAEs trained on LLMs. We suspect that feature hedging may be one of the core reasons that SAEs consistently underperform supervised baselines. Finally, we use our understanding of feature hedging to propose an improved variant of matryoshka SAEs. Importantly, our work shows that SAE width is not a neutral hyperparameter: narrower SAEs suffer more from hedging than wider SAEs.

papers.title: SCIURus: Shared Circuits for Interpretable Uncertainty Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: Do the factuality of generated responses and a model's uncertainty originate in separate or shared circuits within the model architecture?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides strong evidence that a language model's uncertainty and the factuality of its generated answers are produced by shared circuits in the model, rather than separate ones.
papers.conclusion: The results broadly support the shared circuits hypothesis, suggesting that P(IK) probing elicits introspective, interpretable uncertainty estimates and that uncertainty quantification in LLMs may largely rely on the same circuitry used for question-answering.
papers.key_findings:
Causal tracing experiments show that the same model components (layers, attention heads) affect both the model's correct-token probability and the P(IK) probe's confidence estimate.
Zero-ablation experiments (both leave-one-out and COAR) across multiple models and datasets support the shared circuits hypothesis, with changes in model accuracy and probe output being highly correlated.
The P(IK) probe's uncertainty representation often remains calibrated even after interventions that damage model performance.
The shared circuits hypothesis holds across a range of models (Llama 2/3, Gemma 2) and datasets (TriviaQA, WebQuestions, MMLU, ARC, CounterFact).
Some discrepancies occur, such as when answer tokens appear in the question, where restorations can suppress model accuracy but not probe confidence.
papers.limitation:
Zero-ablation may lack specificity because zeroing out a component can severely damage general language coherence, not just task-specific information flow.
Causal tracing may miss important circuits when information flows along multiple parallel paths, as restoring a single path may not show a substantial effect.
future_direction: Analyze the mechanisms responsible for P(IK) estimates in greater detail.
Apply P(IK) probing as an interpretability tool to study phenomena like hallucination in LLMs.
Perform similar analyses on other uncertainty quantification methods, such as verbalized uncertainty.
papers.abstract: Carter Teplica, Yixin Liu, Arman Cohan, Tim G. J. Rudner. Proceedings of the 2025 Conference of the Nations of the Americas Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2025.

papers.title: Mind Scramble: Unveiling Large Language Model Psychology Via Typoglycemia
papers.research_question: Does LLM possess human-like cognitive processes and mechanisms in reading and comprehending? The paper uses Typoglycemia to explore this.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces LLM Psychology, a framework that uses Typoglycemia experiments to study cognitive behaviors of LLMs. It finds that LLMs exhibit human-like behaviors but are fundamentally data-driven, and each LLM has a unique cognitive pattern.
papers.conclusion: The study advances research on aligning LLMs with human cognition and provides evidence that LLMs' abilities are data-driven, offering a case for LLM Psychology.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs demonstrate human-like behaviors on a macro scale, such as slightly lower task accuracy with consuming more tokens and time.
Different LLMs show varying degrees of robustness to scrambled input, making it a democratized benchmark for model evaluation.
The impact of different task types varies, with complex logical tasks (e.g., math) in scrambled format being more challenging.
LLMs' emergent human-like abilities are fundamentally statistical and data-driven, rather than genuinely resembling human cognition.
Each LLM exhibits its unique and consistent 'cognitive pattern' across various tasks, unveiling a general mechanism in its psychology process.
papers.abstract: Research into the external behaviors and internal mechanisms of large language models (LLMs) has shown promise in addressing complex tasks in the physical world. Studies suggest that powerful LLMs, like GPT-4, are beginning to exhibit human-like cognitive abilities, including planning, reasoning, and reflection. In this paper, we introduce a research line and methodology called LLM Psychology, leveraging human psychology experiments to investigate the cognitive behaviors and mechanisms of LLMs. We migrate the Typoglycemia phenomenon from psychology to explore the "mind" of LLMs. Unlike human brains, which rely on context and word patterns to comprehend scrambled text, LLMs use distinct encoding and decoding processes. Through Typoglycemia experiments at the character, word, and sentence levels, we observe: (I) LLMs demonstrate human-like behaviors on a macro scale, such as lower task accuracy and higher token/time consumption; (II) LLMs exhibit varying robustness to scrambled input, making Typoglycemia a benchmark for model evaluation without new datasets; (III) Different task types have varying impacts, with complex logical tasks (e.g., math) being more challenging in scrambled form; (IV) Each LLM has a unique and consistent "cognitive pattern" across tasks, revealing general mechanisms in its psychology process. We provide an in-depth analysis of hidden layers to explain these phenomena, paving the way for future research in LLM Psychology and deeper interpretability.

papers.title: Brittle Minds, Fixable Activations: Understanding Belief Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do internal belief representations emerge in language models? Are they structured or spurious? How robust are they to prompt variations? Can they be strengthened?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that belief representations in language models improve with model size and fine-tuning, are structured yet brittle to prompt variations, and can be strengthened using contrastive activation addition to correct wrong Theory of Mind inferences.
papers.conclusion: Belief representations in language models are structured but brittle, and they can be strengthened via activation editing, offering a path toward more reliable Theory of Mind reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Belief representations emerge in consistent patterns across models, improve with model size, and benefit significantly from fine-tuning, especially in smaller models.
Control tasks and PCA show that belief representations are structured and not spurious.
Representations of others' beliefs are brittle to semantically neutral prompt variations.
Contrastive activation addition (CAA) can strengthen belief representations and improve ToM performance across different tasks.
CAA steering vectors are general and transferable to other ToM tasks, yielding substantial performance gains.
papers.limitation:
The study focused on one dataset (BigToM) and a limited set of model families due to computational constraints.
The approach could be extended to other mental states beyond beliefs.
future_direction: Exploring how different types of fine-tuning influence the emergence of internal belief representations.
Developing robustness benchmarks and new approaches to improve generalization of belief representations.
Directly embedding perspective-taking circuits into model architectures.
papers.abstract: Despite growing interest in Theory of Mind (ToM) tasks for evaluating language models (LMs), little is known about how LMs internally represent mental states of self and others. Understanding these internal mechanisms is critical - not only to move beyond surface-level performance, but also for model alignment and safety, where subtle misattributions of mental states may go undetected in generated outputs. In this work, we present the first systematic investigation of belief representations in LMs by probing models across different scales, training regimens, and prompts - using control tasks to rule out confounds. Our experiments provide evidence that both model size and fine-tuning substantially improve LMs' internal representations of others' beliefs, which are structured - not mere by-products of spurious correlations - yet brittle to prompt variations. Crucially, we show that these representations can be strengthened: targeted edits to model activations can correct wrong ToM inferences.

papers.title: Trick or Neat: Adversarial Ambiguity and Language Model Evaluation
papers.research_question: How well do language models detect linguistic ambiguity, and how is ambiguity encoded in their representations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an adversarial ambiguity dataset (AmbAdv) and shows that linear probes on model representations can decode ambiguity with high accuracy, while direct prompting fails.
papers.conclusion: Linear probes are effective at decoding ambiguity from model representations, while prompting is not robust, and the introduced dataset AmbAdv serves as a challenging benchmark.
papers.key_findings:
Direct prompting fails to robustly identify ambiguity in language models.
Linear probes trained on model representations can decode ambiguity with high accuracy, sometimes exceeding 90%.
Models exhibit a 'yes bias' when prompted for ambiguity identification.
Models struggle with adversarial substitutions, particularly random and rhyme word modifications.
Analysis of disambiguations suggests models may partially rely on memorization to resolve ambiguity.
papers.limitation: LLMs may partially rely on memorization to resolve ambiguity.
papers.abstract: Detecting ambiguity is important for language understanding, including uncertainty estimation, humour detection, and processing garden path sentences.We assess language models' sensitivity to ambiguity by introducing an adversarial ambiguity dataset that includes syntactic, lexical, and phonological ambiguities along with adversarial variations (e.g., word-order changes, synonym replacements, and randombased alterations).Our findings show that direct prompting fails to robustly identify ambiguity, while linear probes trained on model representations can decode ambiguity with high accuracy, sometimes exceeding 90%.Our results offer insights into the prompting paradigm and how language models encode ambiguity at different layers.We release both our code and data:coastalcph/lm_ambiguity.1 Except, of course, if the dress has a mirror.Such exceptions illustrate how pragmatics may override semantics (Morris, 1946), but LLMs must be sensitive to distinctions between syntactic ambiguities that support multiple conventional readings and those typically resolved by context. 2 spaces/lmsys/chatbot-arena-leaderboard 3 jndiogo/LLM-chat-templates 4 We define consistency here as the ability to make reliable decisions in semantically similar contexts demonstrating a systematic capacity to generalize across language variations" (Elazar et al., 2021).saahowwwnem ttwahimitonteehmaww w tntaihotnemh i wttttah h maehinntllehtew w s sttceecitihtolhte e heep stttelcheeh.oelseepcto steecp.loes.lepsec.ope.cope.sub sju_bsysonym | t suj_nbjyn_raonndyomThm | eJe mtneoatcheer ssa omhea ntee wle tsteelec ihcloess t tpheco.oppee

papers.title: Probing the Geometry of Truth: Consistency and Generalization of Truth Directions in LLMs Across Logical Transformations and Question Answering Tasks
papers.research_question: Do LLMs universally represent truthfulness as a linear feature (truth direction)? Are simple probing techniques sufficiently expressive to identify truth directions? How does the truth direction generalize across logical transformations and question answering tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Consistent truth directions only emerge in capable LLMs and can be identified with simple linear probes; these probes generalize effectively to logical transformations, question answering, in-context learning, and external knowledge sources.
papers.conclusion: Truth directions are present in capable LLMs, can be identified with simple probes, and generalize well, highlighting their potential for eliciting latent knowledge and improving trust in LLM outputs.
papers.key_findings:
Not all LLMs exhibit consistent truth directions; this property is correlated with model capability, with stronger representations in more capable models.
Simple probes (linear SVM, logistic regression, MLP, mass-mean) are sufficient to identify truth directions when they exist.
Truthfulness probes generalize across logical negation, conjunction, and disjunction.
Truthfulness probes trained on atomic statements generalize to question answering tasks (MMLU, TriviaQA) and contextual knowledge tasks (SciQ, BoolQ, XSum).
Truthfulness probes can be used for selective question answering to filter out false answers, improving answer quality.
papers.limitation:
The term 'truth' may not be exactly what the probes measure; they likely capture an overlap between widely accepted human beliefs and objective truths.
Generalization is only tested on short-form QA; long-form QA and instruction-following tasks are not studied.
The causality of truthfulness probes is unclear; they may capture spuriously-correlated features rather than the target feature.
Computational resources limited evaluation to models up to Llama-3.1-70B, leaving more advanced models like GPT-4 untested.
future_direction: Extend analysis to more complex scenarios such as long-form QA and instruction-following tasks.
Study the causal implications of truth directions to guide LLMs toward more truthful responses.
Test the hypothesis on more advanced models like GPT-4.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are trained on extensive datasets that encapsulate substantial world knowledge. However, their outputs often include confidently stated inaccuracies. Earlier works suggest that LLMs encode truthfulness as a distinct linear feature, termed the "truth direction", which can classify truthfulness reliably. We address several open questions about the truth direction: (i) whether LLMs universally exhibit consistent truth directions; (ii) whether sophisticated probing techniques are necessary to identify truth directions; and (iii) how the truth direction generalizes across diverse contexts. Our findings reveal that not all LLMs exhibit consistent truth directions, with stronger representations observed in more capable models, particularly in the context of logical negation. Additionally, we demonstrate that truthfulness probes trained on declarative atomic statements can generalize effectively to logical transformations, question-answering tasks, in-context learning, and external knowledge sources. Finally, we explore the practical application of truthfulness probes in selective question-answering, illustrating their potential to improve user trust in LLM outputs. These results advance our understanding of truth directions and provide new insights into the internal representations of LLM beliefs. Our code is public at https://github.com/colored-dye/truthfulness_probe_generalization

papers.title: Calibration Across Layers: Understanding Calibration Evolution in LLMs
papers.research_question: How does calibration evolve throughout the depth of transformer-based language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that calibration is a distributed phenomenon across network layers, with a distinct confidence correction phase in later layers, and identifies a low-dimensional calibration direction in the residual stream that can improve calibration metrics without harming accuracy.
papers.conclusion: Our findings suggest that calibration is a distributed phenomenon, shaped throughout the network’s forward pass, not just in its final projection, providing new insights into how confidence-regulating mechanisms operate within LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Calibration evolves across layers, with a distinct confidence correction phase in later layers where models become overconfident and then recalibrate.
A low-dimensional calibration direction in the residual stream is identified, and perturbing it improves calibration metrics (ECE and MCE) without affecting accuracy.
The unembedding matrix's null space plays a role in calibration.
Calibration is a distributed phenomenon across the network depth, not just in the final projection.
papers.limitation:
The calibration direction identified in Phi-2 does not generalize effectively to Mistral or LLaMA-2.
The analysis is limited to zero-shot MCQA prompts and may not extend to in-context learning settings.
future_direction: Generalizing calibration directions using gradient-based approaches and verifying alignment with low-rank structures in the unembedding matrix.
Investigating model internals to identify neurons or components that contribute to confidence modulation.
Extending analysis to in-context learning settings and cross-model/dataset transferability.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated inherent calibration capabilities, where predicted probabilities align well with correctness, despite prior findings that deep neural networks are often overconfident. Recent studies have linked this behavior to specific components in the final layer, such as entropy neurons and the unembedding matrix null space. In this work, we provide a complementary perspective by investigating how calibration evolves throughout the network depth. Analyzing multiple open-weight models on the MMLU benchmark, we uncover a distinct confidence correction phase in the upper/later layers, where model confidence is actively recalibrated after decision certainty has been reached. Furthermore, we identify a low-dimensional calibration direction in the residual stream whose perturbation significantly improves calibration metrics (ECE and MCE) without harming accuracy. Our findings suggest that calibration is a distributed phenomenon, shaped throughout the network forward pass, not just in its final projection, providing new insights into how confidence-regulating mechanisms operate within LLMs.

papers.title: LLMs Know More Than They Show: On the Intrinsic Representation of LLM Hallucinations
papers.research_question: How much information about truthfulness is encoded in LLMs' internal representations, and how can it be used for error detection and analysis?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode truthfulness information in exact answer tokens, enabling improved error detection and analysis of error types, and revealing that truthfulness encoding is skill-specific rather than universal.
papers.conclusion: Internal representations of LLMs encode rich information about truthfulness and error types, which can guide error analysis and mitigation strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Truthfulness information is concentrated in exact answer tokens, and leveraging this improves error detection performance.
Error detectors based on probing do not generalize across tasks, indicating that truthfulness encoding is skill-specific.
Internal representations can predict error types (e.g., consistently incorrect, many answers).
There is a discrepancy between internal encoding and external behavior: the model may encode the correct answer but generate an incorrect one.
papers.limitation:
Error detectors do not generalize across datasets.
The error taxonomy is non-orthogonal, with overlapping categories.
future_direction: Further investigation is required to disentangle the multiple mechanisms of truthfulness encoding.
Potential directions for improvements in error analysis and mitigation using the model-centric framework.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often produce errors, including factual inaccuracies, biases, and reasoning failures, collectively referred to as "hallucinations". Recent studies have demonstrated that LLMs' internal states encode information regarding the truthfulness of their outputs, and that this information can be utilized to detect errors. In this work, we show that the internal representations of LLMs encode much more information about truthfulness than previously recognized. We first discover that the truthfulness information is concentrated in specific tokens, and leveraging this property significantly enhances error detection performance. Yet, we show that such error detectors fail to generalize across datasets, implying that -- contrary to prior claims -- truthfulness encoding is not universal but rather multifaceted. Next, we show that internal representations can also be used for predicting the types of errors the model is likely to make, facilitating the development of tailored mitigation strategies. Lastly, we reveal a discrepancy between LLMs' internal encoding and external behavior: they may encode the correct answer, yet consistently generate an incorrect one. Taken together, these insights deepen our understanding of LLM errors from the model's internal perspective, which can guide future research on enhancing error analysis and mitigation.

papers.title: Large Language Models Must Be Taught to Know What They Don't Know
papers.research_question: How can we obtain reliable uncertainty estimates from large language models (LLMs) for their predictions, particularly in open-ended generation tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning LLMs on a small dataset of correct and incorrect answers using LoRA produces well-calibrated uncertainty estimates that generalize across distribution shifts and improves human-AI collaboration.
papers.conclusion: Large language models must be explicitly taught to know what they don't know, and fine-tuning on a small calibration dataset is an effective and efficient method to achieve reliable uncertainty estimation.
papers.key_findings:
Prompting alone is insufficient for good calibration in open-ended generation tasks.
Fine-tuning on as few as 1000 graded examples outperforms baseline uncertainty estimation methods.
Training through the model's features (e.g., using LoRA) is necessary for good performance and generalization, especially in open-ended settings.
Models can be used as general-purpose uncertainty estimators, applicable not just to their own predictions but also to the predictions of other models.
Providing uncertainty estimates to users in a human-AI collaboration setting improves their reliance sensibility and task performance.
papers.abstract: When using large language models (LLMs) in high-stakes applications, we need to know when we can trust their predictions. Some works argue that prompting high-performance LLMs is sufficient to produce calibrated uncertainties, while others introduce sampling methods that can be prohibitively expensive. In this work, we first argue that prompting on its own is insufficient to achieve good calibration and then show that fine-tuning on a small dataset of correct and incorrect answers can create an uncertainty estimate with good generalization and small computational overhead. We show that a thousand graded examples are sufficient to outperform baseline methods and that training through the features of a model is necessary for good performance and tractable for large open-source models when using LoRA. We also investigate the mechanisms that enable reliable LLM uncertainty estimation, finding that many models can be used as general-purpose uncertainty estimators, applicable not just to their own uncertainties but also the uncertainty of other models. Lastly, we show that uncertainty estimates inform human use of LLMs in human-AI collaborative settings through a user study.

papers.title: What Large Language Models Know and What People Think They Know
papers.research_question: How large is the gap between LLM model confidence and human confidence (calibration gap) and the gap in ability to discriminate correct/incorrect answers (discrimination gap)? Can these gaps be reduced by adapting LLM textual output to internal model confidence?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that users overestimate LLM accuracy with default explanations, and that tailoring explanations to reflect the model's internal confidence narrows the calibration and discrimination gaps, improving user perception of LLM accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The study underscores the importance of accurate uncertainty communication from LLMs and shows that tailoring explanations to internal confidence can bridge the gap between what LLMs know and what people think they know.
papers.key_findings:
Users tend to overestimate the accuracy of LLM responses when provided with default explanations.
Longer explanations increase user confidence even when they do not improve answer accuracy.
By adjusting LLM explanations to better reflect the models’ internal confidence, both the calibration gap and the discrimination gap narrow.
Participants lack specialized knowledge and their accuracy is similar to the LLM's accuracy.
Self-assessed expertise does not affect performance in estimating LLM accuracy.
papers.limitation: Focus on a specific type of question (multiple choice and short answer) with a small number of response alternatives.
papers.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) systems, particularly large language models (LLMs), become increasingly integrated into decision-making processes, the ability to trust their outputs is crucial. To earn human trust, LLMs must be well calibrated such that they can accurately assess and communicate the likelihood of their predictions being correct. Whereas recent work has focused on LLMs' internal confidence, less is understood about how effectively they convey uncertainty to users. Here we explore the calibration gap, which refers to the difference between human confidence in LLM-generated answers and the models' actual confidence, and the discrimination gap, which reflects how well humans and models can distinguish between correct and incorrect answers. Our experiments with multiple-choice and short-answer questions reveal that users tend to overestimate the accuracy of LLM responses when provided with default explanations. Moreover, longer explanations increased user confidence, even when the extra length did not improve answer accuracy. By adjusting LLM explanations to better reflect the models' internal confidence, both the calibration gap and the discrimination gap narrowed, significantly improving user perception of LLM accuracy. These findings underscore the importance of accurate uncertainty communication and highlight the effect of explanation length in influencing user trust in AI-assisted decision-making environments. Code and Data can be found at https://osf.io/y7pr6/ . Journal publication can be found on Nature Machine Intelligence at https://www.nature.com/articles/s42256-024-00976-7 .

papers.title: Neural Natural Language Inference Models Partially Embed Theories of Lexical Entailment and Negation
papers.research_question: Whether neural models for Natural Language Inference (NLI) can learn the compositional interactions between lexical entailment and negation.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that a BERT-based model, after fine-tuning, can learn to reason about lexical entailment and negation, and structural evaluations (probes and interventions) provide evidence that the model partially embeds the target monotonicity algorithm.
papers.conclusion: The BERT model at least partially embeds a theory of lexical entailment and negation at an algorithmic level, in addition to achieving the correct input-output behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Models trained on general-purpose NLI datasets (SNLI/MNLI) fail systematically on examples requiring negation to reverse lexical entailment.
Fine-tuning on a subset of the MoNLI dataset enables models to solve a systematic generalization task requiring lexical entailment and negation.
Probing experiments show that BERT's internal representations correlate with the lexical entailment relation and the algorithm's output.
Interchange intervention experiments show that BERT's causal dynamics mirror the monotonicity algorithm on specific subsets of the MoNLI data.
papers.limitation:
The interchange intervention methodology is not yet formally grounded.
The analysis only shows that BERT mimics the algorithm on subsets of MoNLI, not on the entire dataset.
papers.abstract: We address whether neural models for Natural Language Inference (NLI) can learn the compositional interactions between lexical entailment and negation, using four methods: the behavioral evaluation methods of (1) challenge test sets and (2) systematic generalization tasks, and the structural evaluation methods of (3) probes and (4) interventions. To facilitate this holistic evaluation, we present Monotonicity NLI (MoNLI), a new naturalistic dataset focused on lexical entailment and negation. In our behavioral evaluations, we find that models trained on general-purpose NLI datasets fail systematically on MoNLI examples containing negation, but that MoNLI fine-tuning addresses this failure. In our structural evaluations, we look for evidence that our top-performing BERT-based model has learned to implement the monotonicity algorithm behind MoNLI. Probes yield evidence consistent with this conclusion, and our intervention experiments bolster this, showing that the causal dynamics of the model mirror the causal dynamics of this algorithm on subsets of MoNLI. This suggests that the BERT model at least partially embeds a theory of lexical entailment and negation at an algorithmic level.

papers.title: Revisiting Prompt Sensitivity in Large Language Models for Text Classification: The Role of Prompt Underspecification
papers.research_question: Is a significant portion of the observed prompt sensitivity in LLMs attributable to prompt underspecification, and how can it be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that prompt underspecification is a significant contributor to observed prompt sensitivity in LLMs, and that using well-specified instruction prompts and in-context learning can effectively mitigate this issue.
papers.conclusion: A large part of observed prompt sensitivity is due to the use of underspecified prompts, and this can be effectively addressed by using well-specified instruction prompts and in-context learning, leading to more robust LLM evaluations.
papers.key_findings:
Underspecified prompts exhibit higher performance variance and lower logit values for relevant label tokens compared to instruction prompts.
In-context learning provides the most consistent benefit for mitigating prompt sensitivity and underspecification, especially when combined with instruction-tuned models.
Logit analysis shows that higher label token logit values are a good indicator of prompt quality and correlate with higher accuracy.
Linear probe analysis reveals that internal model representations are only marginally affected by prompt underspecification, with performance issues emerging primarily in the final layers.
Calibration provides similar but less consistent improvements than in-context learning, while the UNK token mitigation strategy often degrades performance.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to three datasets and three model families, which may not generalize to all tasks and models.
Generation evaluation uses simple string matching and regex, which may underestimate model capabilities.
The analysis uses 10 prompt variants per setting, which may not capture the full spectrum of prompt sensitivity.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used as zero-shot and few-shot classifiers, where task behaviour is largely controlled through prompting. A growing number of works have observed that LLMs are sensitive to prompt variations, with small changes leading to large changes in performance. However, in many cases, the investigation of sensitivity is performed using underspecified prompts that provide minimal task instructions and weakly constrain the model's output space. In this work, we argue that a significant portion of the observed prompt sensitivity can be attributed to prompt underspecification. We systematically study and compare the sensitivity of underspecified prompts and prompts that provide specific instructions. Utilising performance analysis, logit analysis, and linear probing, we find that underspecified prompts exhibit higher performance variance and lower logit values for relevant tokens, while instruction-prompts suffer less from such problems. However, linear probing analysis suggests that the effects of prompt underspecification have only a marginal impact on the internal LLM representations, instead emerging in the final layers. Overall, our findings highlight the need for more rigour when investigating and mitigating prompt sensitivity.

papers.title: Measuring and Analyzing Intelligence via Contextual Uncertainty in Large Language Models using Information-Theoretic Metrics
papers.research_question: How do large language models process information as context length grows? The paper investigates this by building a quantitative Cognitive Profile for any model using information-theoretic metrics.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a task-agnostic method for building a quantitative Cognitive Profile of LLMs by tracking predictive uncertainty (via the Entropy Decay Curve) and summarizing it with the Information Gain Span, which reveals how models process information and can detect memorization.
papers.conclusion: The Entropy Decay Curve and Information Gain Span offer a principled, task-agnostic way to analyze and compare the internal dynamics of LLMs, revealing differences in how models process information and flagging potential memorization.
papers.key_findings:
Larger models (like Llama 3.3 70.6B) show a sharper decline in uncertainty with context length compared to smaller models.
The Entropy Decay Curve (EDC) is corpus-dependent: easier texts (like Alice's Adventures in Wonderland) lead to lower long-context uncertainty than more complex texts (like Ulysses and Kant's Critique of Judgement).
The EDC can detect memorization (entropy collapse) when long-context uncertainty becomes extremely low, indicating potential data contamination.
The Information Gain Span (IGS) provides a single scalar that summarizes the desirability of the decay pattern (high initial uncertainty and low final uncertainty).
The method provides a quantitative way to compare models and texts without task-specific benchmarks.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to a small set of models, corpora, and window lengths, and relies on finite-sample Monte Carlo estimates.
future_direction: Extend coverage to more architectures and training regimes.
Evaluate specialized domains (code, scientific, medical, legal).
Characterize estimator variance and sensitivity to sampling design, and refine contamination tests by combining EDC signals with independent memorization audits.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) excel on many task-specific benchmarks, yet the mechanisms that drive this success remain poorly understood. We move from asking what these systems can do to asking how they process information. Our contribution is a task-agnostic method that builds a quantitative Cognitive Profile for any model. The profile is built around the Entropy Decay Curve -- a plot of a model's normalised predictive uncertainty as context length grows. Across several state-of-the-art LLMs and diverse texts, the curves expose distinctive, stable profiles that depend on both model scale and text complexity. We also propose the Information Gain Span (IGS) as a single index that summarises the desirability of a decay pattern. Together, these tools offer a principled way to analyse and compare the internal dynamics of modern AI systems.

papers.title: ShortGPT: Layers in Large Language Models are More Redundant Than You Expect
papers.research_question: How redundant are the layers in large language models, and can a simple layer removal method based on a new importance metric effectively prune them?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies significant layer redundancy in LLMs and introduces Block Influence (BI) to measure layer importance. Based on BI, the proposed ShortGPT method removes redundant layers, achieving competitive pruning results without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit significant layer-wise redundancy, and a simple pruning method based on layer removal (ShortGPT) can effectively compress models with minimal performance loss, offering insights for future model compression and training efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Layers in LLMs are redundant, especially in the middle to later layers, and removing them individually causes minimal performance degradation.
The proposed Block Influence (BI) metric, based on cosine similarity between a layer's input and output hidden states, correlates with layer importance.
ShortGPT, a simple layer removal method based on BI, outperforms previous state-of-the-art pruning methods and maintains ~90% performance while reducing ~25% parameters.
The redundancy phenomenon is not unique to transformers; it also exists in non-transformer models like Mamba and RWKV.
ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization and can be combined with it for further compression.
papers.limitation: Layer removal has a more significant negative effect on generative tasks compared to multiple-choice tasks, especially for smaller models.
future_direction: Exploring post-training to restore performance after pruning
Improving model training efficiency by reducing inherent redundancy
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance in performance, their size has escalated significantly, with current LLMs containing billions or even trillions of parameters. However, in this study, we discovered that many layers of LLMs exhibit high similarity, and some layers play a negligible role in network functionality. Based on this observation, we define a metric called Block Influence (BI) to gauge the significance of each layer in LLMs. We then propose a straightforward pruning approach: layer removal, in which we directly delete the redundant layers in LLMs based on their BI scores. Experiments demonstrate that our method, which we call ShortGPT, significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods in model pruning. Moreover, ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization-like methods, enabling further reduction in parameters and computation. The ability to achieve better results through simple layer removal, as opposed to more complex pruning techniques, suggests a high degree of redundancy in the model architecture.

papers.title: Uncovering Uncertainty in Transformer Inference
papers.research_question: How do transformer models iteratively refine predictions during inference, and can cross-entropy-based metrics detect uncertainty in token generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides empirical support for the Iterative Inference Hypothesis in transformers and introduces a cross-entropy-based method to detect uncertainty during token generation, showing distinct differences between correct and incorrect outputs.
papers.conclusion: The paper supports the Iterative Inference Hypothesis and demonstrates that cross-entropy-based metrics can detect uncertainty in transformer token generation, with potential for flagging hallucinations.
papers.key_findings:
The nth token embedding in the residual stream follows a trajectory of decreasing loss, supporting the Iterative Inference Hypothesis.
Cross-entropy between residual predictions and target distributions shows observable differences between correct and incorrect generations.
Output cross-entropy with respect to the sampled token is a strong predictor of correctness on the idiom dataset, with an AUC of 0.92.
Cross-entropy metrics capture uncertainty in open-ended generations, with spikes corresponding to erroneous or uncertain tokens.
papers.limitation: The cross-entropy measure captures both prompt-inherent and model uncertainty, and cannot disambiguate between them; it also fails for confidently incorrect models.
future_direction: Expanding analysis to a broad range of datasets and language models of varying sizes.
Extending the study to multi-token generations.
Exploring additional convergence metrics for predicting correct versus incorrect generations.
papers.abstract: We explore the Iterative Inference Hypothesis (IIH) within the context of transformer-based language models, aiming to understand how a model's latent representations are progressively refined and whether observable differences are present between correct and incorrect generations. Our findings provide empirical support for the IIH, showing that the nth token embedding in the residual stream follows a trajectory of decreasing loss. Additionally, we observe that the rate at which residual embeddings converge to a stable output representation reflects uncertainty in the token generation process. Finally, we introduce a method utilizing cross-entropy to detect this uncertainty and demonstrate its potential to distinguish between correct and incorrect token generations on a dataset of idioms.

papers.title: Reasoning as State Transition: A Representational Analysis of Reasoning Evolution in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How does reasoning ability evolve during training in large language models, and what is the role of internal representation dynamics in this process?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a representational analysis framework showing that post-training yields limited improvement in static initial representation quality, but reasoning involves a continuous distributional shift in representations during generation, which post-training enhances to drive representations toward a better state for task solving.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a novel representational perspective on reasoning evolution in LLMs, highlighting the importance of internal state dynamics and the role of post-training in enhancing state transitions, offering insights for future model analysis and optimization.
papers.key_findings:
Post-training yields only limited improvement in static initial representation quality.
Reasoning involves a significant continuous distributional shift in representations during generation, unlike non-reasoning tasks.
Post-training empowers models to drive this representation transition toward a better distribution for task solving.
There is a high correlation between generation correctness and final representations, but low correlation with initial representations.
The semantic content of the generated tokens is the dominant driver of the state transition, not additional computation or intrinsic parameter differences.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models have achieved remarkable performance on reasoning tasks, motivating research into how this ability evolves during training. Prior work has primarily analyzed this evolution via explicit generation outcomes, treating the reasoning process as a black box and obscuring internal changes. To address this opacity, we introduce a representational perspective to investigate the dynamics of the model's internal states. Through comprehensive experiments across models at various training stages, we discover that post-training yields only limited improvement in static initial representation quality. Furthermore, we reveal that, distinct from non-reasoning tasks, reasoning involves a significant continuous distributional shift in representations during generation. Comparative analysis indicates that post-training empowers models to drive this transition toward a better distribution for task solving. To clarify the relationship between internal states and external outputs, statistical analysis confirms a high correlation between generation correctness and the final representations; while counterfactual experiments identify the semantics of the generated tokens, rather than additional computation during inference or intrinsic parameter differences, as the dominant driver of the transition. Collectively, we offer a novel understanding of the reasoning process and the effect of training on reasoning enhancement, providing valuable insights for future model analysis and optimization.

papers.title: When Thinking LLMs Lie: Unveiling the Strategic Deception in Representations of Reasoning Models
papers.research_question: How can strategic deception in chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning models be induced, detected, and controlled?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework using representation engineering to systematically induce, detect, and control strategic deception in CoT-enabled LLMs, achieving high detection accuracy and successful intervention.
papers.conclusion: The work unveils the specific honesty-related issue of reasoning models and provides tools for inducing, detecting, and controlling strategic deception, contributing to trustworthy AI alignment.
papers.key_findings:
CoT models exhibit intrinsic strategic deception capabilities even without explicit prompting in certain contexts.
A representation-based detection method using Linear Artificial Tomography (LAT) achieves 89% accuracy in identifying deception.
Activation steering using extracted deception vectors can induce context-appropriate deception with a 40% success rate without explicit prompts.
The deception rate under threat-based prompts is consistently slightly lower than the model's truth-telling accuracy on the same factual datasets.
Steering vector interventions can induce unfaithful chain-of-thought reasoning, where harmful choices become obscured within the reasoning process.
papers.abstract: The honesty of large language models (LLMs) is a critical alignment challenge, especially as advanced systems with chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning may strategically deceive humans. Unlike traditional honesty issues on LLMs, which could be possibly explained as some kind of hallucination, those models' explicit thought paths enable us to study strategic deception--goal-driven, intentional misinformation where reasoning contradicts outputs. Using representation engineering, we systematically induce, detect, and control such deception in CoT-enabled LLMs, extracting "deception vectors" via Linear Artificial Tomography (LAT) for 89% detection accuracy. Through activation steering, we achieve a 40% success rate in eliciting context-appropriate deception without explicit prompts, unveiling the specific honesty-related issue of reasoning models and providing tools for trustworthy AI alignment.

papers.title: The Curious Case of Analogies: Investigating Analogical Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode and apply high-level relational concepts for analogical reasoning, and how do they structurally align analogous situations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper investigates the internal mechanisms of analogical reasoning in LLMs, finding that they encode relational information in mid-upper layers but struggle to apply it, and that successful reasoning is associated with strong structural alignment between analogous situations.
papers.conclusion: LLMs show emerging but limited capabilities in analogical reasoning, with parallels to human cognition in encoding relational information and structural alignment, but gaps in application and alignment.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs effectively encode underlying relationships between analogous entities in mid-upper layers, with relational information being a key factor for correct reasoning.
LLMs struggle not only when relational information is missing but also when attempting to apply it to new entities.
Strategically patching hidden representations at critical token positions can facilitate information transfer and improve performance.
Successful analogical reasoning is marked by strong structural alignment between analogous situations, while failures show degraded alignment.
Analogical structure becomes linearly separable in middle layers, and token-level alignment (measured by Mutual Alignment Score) is higher for correct analogies.
future_direction: Future research into understanding and improving the analogical reasoning capabilities of LLMs.
papers.abstract: Analogical reasoning is at the core of human cognition, serving as an important foundation for a variety of intellectual activities. While prior work has shown that LLMs can represent task patterns and surface-level concepts, it remains unclear whether these models can encode high-level relational concepts and apply them to novel situations through structured comparisons. In this work, we explore this fundamental aspect using proportional and story analogies, and identify three key findings. First, LLMs effectively encode the underlying relationships between analogous entities; both attributive and relational information propagate through mid-upper layers in correct cases, whereas reasoning failures reflect missing relational information within these layers. Second, unlike humans, LLMs often struggle not only when relational information is missing, but also when attempting to apply it to new entities. In such cases, strategically patching hidden representations at critical token positions can facilitate information transfer to a certain extent. Lastly, successful analogical reasoning in LLMs is marked by strong structural alignment between analogous situations, whereas failures often reflect degraded or misplaced alignment. Overall, our findings reveal that LLMs exhibit emerging but limited capabilities in encoding and applying high-level relational concepts, highlighting both parallels and gaps with human cognition.

papers.title: Overthinking the Truth: Understanding how Language Models Process False Demonstrations
papers.research_question: Why do language models imitate incorrect demonstrations in their context, and how does this behavior emerge internally?
papers.core_contribution: Language models 'overthink' when given false few-shot demonstrations, and this harmful imitation is caused by specific 'false induction heads' in late layers that attend to and copy incorrect labels from the context.
papers.conclusion: Studying intermediate model computations, such as through the logit lens and head ablation, is a promising avenue for understanding and mitigating harmful context-following behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
Given incorrect demonstrations, model accuracy decreases in later layers after a 'critical layer', a phenomenon termed 'overthinking'.
Ablating late layers or specific attention heads improves accuracy on incorrect demonstrations, indicating these components are responsible for the harmful imitation.
False induction heads are identified as attention heads in late layers that attend to and promote false labels from previous demonstrations.
Ablating a small set of false induction heads reduces the accuracy gap between correct and incorrect prompts by an average of 38.9% across 14 datasets.
The overthinking phenomenon and the role of false induction heads are consistent across multiple model families and sizes.
future_direction: Building tools to understand intermediate computations to proactively understand and reduce harmful model behaviors.
Applying insights to detect and guard against prompt injection attacks.
papers.abstract: Modern language models can imitate complex patterns through few-shot learning, enabling them to complete challenging tasks without fine-tuning. However, imitation can also lead models to reproduce inaccuracies or harmful content if present in the context. We study harmful imitation through the lens of a model's internal representations, and identify two related phenomena: "overthinking" and "false induction heads". The first phenomenon, overthinking, appears when we decode predictions from intermediate layers, given correct vs. incorrect few-shot demonstrations. At early layers, both demonstrations induce similar model behavior, but the behavior diverges sharply at some "critical layer", after which the accuracy given incorrect demonstrations progressively decreases. The second phenomenon, false induction heads, are a possible mechanistic cause of overthinking: these are heads in late layers that attend to and copy false information from previous demonstrations, and whose ablation reduces overthinking. Beyond scientific understanding, our results suggest that studying intermediate model computations could be a promising avenue for understanding and guarding against harmful model behaviors.

papers.title: Toward Better Generalisation in Uncertainty Estimators: Leveraging Data-Agnostic Features
papers.research_question: Can supplementing hidden-state features with data-agnostic features improve the probe’s generalisation to unseen tasks or datasets? Does pruning to the top-ranked hidden-state features amplify this generalisation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper investigates whether incorporating data-agnostic features (probability- and entropy-based metrics) with hidden-state features improves the generalization of uncertainty estimators across tasks and datasets, and whether feature selection on hidden states amplifies this effect.
papers.conclusion: Integrating data-agnostic features with hidden-state features can enhance the generalization of uncertainty estimators, and feature selection can amplify this effect, but the approach underperforms on certain transfer pairs, particularly involving Commonsense Reasoning datasets, where the probe fails to prioritize the data-agnostic features.
papers.key_findings:
Incorporating data-agnostic features generally improves generalization performance, especially for short-form question answering datasets, but fails in some cases involving Commonsense Reasoning datasets.
Feature selection (retaining top-k hidden-state features) can amplify the contribution of data-agnostic features and yield additional gains, but the expected ordering of improvement does not always hold.
Analysis using SHAP values reveals that in successful cases, data-agnostic features are highly ranked, but in failure cases (e.g., with SWAG and Winogrande datasets) they are underweighted or sparsely ranked.
Probes trained solely on hidden-state features generalize poorly across tasks and datasets, indicating overfitting to dataset-specific features.
Factual QA and Reading Comprehension tasks show better cross-generalization, likely because their hidden-state representations are more similar, as suggested by PCA visualization.
papers.limitation:
The data-agnostic features were randomly selected without investigating whether all are effective or if including more/less would affect performance.
The rate of correct answers being misclassified when incorporating data-agnostic features is relatively high.
The baseline (without data-agnostic features) drifts slightly across the three probe configurations, introducing instability in comparisons.
The probe underweights data-agnostic features in Commonsense Reasoning datasets, suggesting their hidden states may already encode similar information.
future_direction: Systematically examine the effectiveness of individual data-agnostic features and the impact of including more or less of them.
Investigate the high rate of correct answers being misclassified when data-agnostic features are added.
Compare the proposed accuracy probe with the semantic entropy probe for generalization performance.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often generate responses that are factually incorrect yet expressed with high confidence, which can pose serious risks for end users. To address this, it is essential for LLMs not only to produce answers but also to provide accurate estimates of their correctness. Uncertainty quantification methods have been introduced to assess the quality of LLM outputs, with factual accuracy being a key aspect of that quality. Among these methods, those that leverage hidden states to train probes have shown particular promise, as these internal representations encode information relevant to the factuality of responses, making this approach the focus of this paper. However, the probe trained on the hidden states of one dataset often struggles to generalise to another dataset of a different task or domain. To address this limitation, we explore combining data-agnostic features with hidden-state features and assess whether this hybrid feature set enhances out-of-domain performance. We further examine whether selecting only the most informative hidden-state features, thereby discarding task-specific noise, enables the data-agnostic features to contribute more effectively. The experiment results indicate that although introducing data-agnostic features generally enhances generalisation performance in most cases, in certain scenarios their inclusion degrades performance. A similar pattern emerges when retaining only the most important hidden-state features - adding data-agnostic features does not consistently further enhance performance compared to using the full set of hidden-state features. A closer analysis reveals that, in some specific cases, the trained probe underweights the data-agnostic features relative to the hidden-state features, which we believe is the main reason why the results are inconclusive.

papers.title: Think-to-Talk or Talk-to-Think? When LLMs Come Up with an Answer in Multi-Hop Arithmetic Reasoning
papers.research_question: When during chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning do LLMs determine their final answer, and how causally dependent is the answer on the CoT explanation?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs compute answers iteratively during CoT generation, and the CoT explanations are faithful reflections of their internal computation, not post-hoc justifications.
papers.conclusion: LLMs compute answers iteratively during CoT, making CoT explanations faithful to the internal reasoning process.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs do not determine the final answer before CoT begins; instead, they compute sub-answers during CoT generation.
Linear probes show that answers become linearly separable in hidden states only after corresponding reasoning steps in CoT.
Causal interventions show that the final answer depends causally on the CoT part, especially the latter steps, showing recency bias.
The model's internal reasoning follows a recency bias: each step causally depends on the previous step.
For distractors (unnecessary variables), the model does not encode them in a linearly separable form, indicating efficient internal mechanisms.
papers.limitation:
The study uses synthetic arithmetic tasks, which may not generalize to natural language reasoning.
The cause of incorrect answers in some instances remains unclear.
future_direction: Investigate more complex and natural language reasoning tasks.
Detailed analysis of error cases and internal representations of digits.
papers.abstract: This study investigates the incremental, internal problem-solving process of language models (LMs) with arithmetic multi-hop reasoning as a case study. We specifically investigate when LMs internally resolve sub/whole problems through first reading the problem statements, generating reasoning chains, and achieving the final answer to mechanistically interpret LMs' multi-hop problem-solving process. Our experiments reveal a systematic incremental reasoning strategy underlying LMs. They have not derived an answer at the moment they first read the problem; instead, they obtain (sub)answers while generating the reasoning chain. Therefore, the generated reasoning chains can be regarded as faithful reflections of the model's internal computation.

papers.title: On the Generalizability of "Competition of Mechanisms: Tracing How Language Models Handle Facts and Counterfactuals"
papers.research_question: Does the competition of mechanisms between factual recall and counterfactual repetition, as identified by Ortu et al. (2024), generalize to larger models, different prompt structures, and across domains?
papers.core_contribution: The attention head ablation method from Ortu et al. (2024) does not generalize well; its effectiveness varies significantly with model architecture, prompt structure, and domain.
papers.conclusion: The competition of mechanisms identified by Ortu et al. (2024) is not fully generalizable; experimental findings in mechanistic interpretability are highly dependent on the specific model, prompt structure, and domain.
papers.key_findings:
Successfully reproduced the original findings on GPT-2 small and Pythia 6.9B regarding positional information encoding, attention block dominance, and attention head specialization.
In Llama 3.1 8B, attention head specialization is greatly reduced, and the logit lens method shows limited early-layer activity and a sharp final-layer activation.
Changing the prompt structure to a question-answering format reduces the model's propensity to repeat the counterfactual, indicating sensitivity to repetition.
The choice of premise word (e.g., 'Redefine', 'Validate') affects the rate of factual vs. counterfactual predictions and the effectiveness of attention head ablation.
The effectiveness of the proposed attention head ablation varies across domains; it works best for domains where the factual token is leaked in the subject (e.g., 'Autos and Vehicles') and fails for others.
papers.limitation:
The logit lens method may be unreliable for larger models like Llama 3.1 8B, potentially failing to capture early-layer mechanisms.
The filtered MQuAKE dataset used for domain analysis is very small (228 prompts), limiting definitive conclusions.
Most extended findings rely on GPT-2 small and a dataset derived from Ortu et al. (2024), limiting generalizability to other models and datasets.
future_direction: Investigate whether larger models distribute work more evenly across heads or if newer interpretability techniques (e.g., circuit analysis, tuned lens) are needed to capture their mechanisms.
Conduct a deeper analysis of why certain dataset domains impact attention head activation, distinguishing between token leakage, topic words, and task difficulty.
Extend the findings to different, larger datasets and models, as well as new prompt structures and premise words.
papers.abstract: We present a reproduction study of "Competition of Mechanisms: Tracing How Language Models Handle Facts and Counterfactuals" (Ortu et al., 2024), which investigates competition of mechanisms in language models between factual recall and counterfactual in-context repetition. Our study successfully reproduces their primary findings regarding the localization of factual and counterfactual information, the dominance of attention blocks in mechanism competition, and the specialization of attention heads in handling competing information. We reproduce their results on both GPT-2 (Radford et al., 2019) and Pythia 6.9B (Biderman et al., 2023). We extend their work in three significant directions. First, we explore the generalizability of these findings to even larger models by replicating the experiments on Llama 3.1 8B (Grattafiori et al., 2024), discovering greatly reduced attention head specialization. Second, we investigate the impact of prompt structure by introducing variations where we avoid repeating the counterfactual statement verbatim or we change the premise word, observing a marked decrease in the logit for the counterfactual token. Finally, we test the validity of the authors' claims for prompts of specific domains, discovering that certain categories of prompts skew the results by providing the factual prediction token as part of the subject of the sentence. Overall, we find that the attention head ablation proposed in Ortu et al. (2024) is ineffective for domains that are underrepresented in their dataset, and that the effectiveness varies based on model architecture, prompt structure, domain and task.

papers.title: Too Big to Fool: Resisting Deception in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do language models of varying capacities within the same family balance in-context information against their internal world models, particularly when faced with intentionally misleading prompts?
papers.core_contribution: Larger language models exhibit greater resilience to deceptive prompts, demonstrating an advanced ability to integrate conflicting in-context information with their internal knowledge, without simply ignoring prompts or relying on memorization.
papers.conclusion: The paper introduces an evaluation strategy that re-uses existing benchmarks with minimal changes to study LLM behavior. Experiments show that larger models are more resilient to deceptive prompts, indicating a better ability to integrate prompt information with internal knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Larger models consistently show a smaller Relative Accuracy Drop when given deceptive hints, indicating higher resilience to misinformation.
Larger models do not ignore in-context information; they effectively follow legitimate instructions and utilize truthful hints.
The resilience is not due to memorization, as shown by control experiments with overfitted models and a model without prior exposure to the test data.
Larger models generally exhibit better instruction-following capabilities, except for the Gemma family which is an outlier.
Models can infer missing information from answer choices, maintaining accuracy above chance even when the question is removed.
papers.limitation:
The study focused exclusively on multiple-choice datasets, which may not capture nuances of open-ended or generative tasks.
Experiments involved only open-source LLMs, limiting generalizability to proprietary models with different architectures or training.
papers.abstract: Large language models must balance their weight-encoded knowledge with in-context information from prompts to generate accurate responses. This paper investigates this interplay by analyzing how models of varying capacities within the same family handle intentionally misleading in-context information. Our experiments demonstrate that larger models exhibit higher resilience to deceptive prompts, showcasing an advanced ability to interpret and integrate prompt information with their internal knowledge. Furthermore, we find that larger models outperform smaller ones in following legitimate instructions, indicating that their resilience is not due to disregarding in-context information. We also show that this phenomenon is likely not a result of memorization but stems from the models' ability to better leverage implicit task-relevant information from the prompt alongside their internally stored knowledge.

papers.title: Correctness-Optimized Residual Activation Lens (CORAL): Transferrable and Calibration-Aware Inference-Time Steering
papers.research_question: How can we improve both accuracy and calibration of LLMs during inference by directly steering using correctness signals from internal activations, rather than optimizing proxies?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CORAL, a lightweight inference-time steering method that uses regularized MLP probes on residual activations to improve accuracy and calibration in MCQA tasks, with demonstrated transferability across benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: CORAL provides a compute-efficient, transferable, and calibration-aware approach to improve MCQA performance during inference by extracting distributed correctness signals via regularized probes.
papers.key_findings:
CORAL consistently improves accuracy and calibration across three 7B models and multiple MCQA benchmarks.
CORAL's learned steering directions transfer without retraining to four held-out benchmarks, averaging 14% accuracy and 49% ECE improvements.
Correctness signals are distributed across many neurons and require supervised aggregation; sparse methods like SAE fail to capture them.
Middle layers (17-21) contain the most useful correctness signals for steering.
Regularized probes capture distributed correctness signals that sparse methods miss.
papers.limitation:
Limited to multiple-choice question answering; generalization to free-form generation is open.
Requires labeled data to train probes, which may not be available for all domains or languages.
Adds inference latency due to activation extraction and probe prediction.
Transfer performance depends on similarity between source and target tasks; dissimilar tasks yield smaller improvements.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit persistent miscalibration, especially after instruction tuning and preference alignment. Modified training objectives can improve calibration, but retraining is expensive. Inference-time steering offers a lightweight alternative, yet most existing methods optimize proxies for correctness rather than correctness itself. We introduce CORAL (Correctness-Optimized Residual Activation Lens), a regularized inference-time steering method that captures distributed correctness signals from model internal activations using weight-decay MLP probes. We evaluate CORAL across three 7B-parameter models and find that it consistently improves accuracy by 10\% and expected calibration error (ECE) by 50\% on average. We additionally demonstrate that these gains transfer without retraining to the complete published test sets of four held-out benchmarks (ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, Math-MC, OpenBookQA), averaging 14\% accuracy improvements and 49\% ECE improvements. Our results support the hypothesis that distributed information in model internals can be extracted using regularized probes when individual neurons are insufficient. CORAL thus provides a compute-efficient, transferable, and calibration-aware approach to improve MCQA performance during inference.

papers.title: Truth-value judgment in language models:belief directions are context sensitive
papers.research_question: How does context impact the behavior of belief probes (directions predictive of truth) in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates the context sensitivity and consistency of belief probes across layers and models, shows belief directions are causal mediators in natural language inference, and introduces a more stable variant of Contrast Consistent Search (CCR).
papers.conclusion: The results suggest that belief directions are causal mediators in the inference process that incorporates in-context information.
papers.key_findings:
Belief probes are generally context sensitive but are also sensitive to irrelevant contexts and can update probabilities incorrectly.
The type of errors made by probes depend on the layer, the model type, and the kind of data.
Belief directions are (one of the) causal mediators in the inference process that incorporates in-context information.
Instruction-tuning makes models more likely to represent prior assertions as true, even if they conflict with the model's own evaluation.
papers.limitation: The difficulty of separating hypothetical LLM 'beliefs' from commonly-held beliefs, as probes might identify features correlated with truth in the training data rather than an objective evaluation of truth.
papers.abstract: Recent work has demonstrated that the latent spaces of large language models (LLMs) contain directions predictive of the truth of sentences. Multiple methods recover such directions and build probes that are described as getting at a model's "knowledge" or "beliefs". We investigate this phenomenon, looking closely at the impact of context on the probes. Our experiments establish where in the LLM the probe's predictions can be described as being conditional on the preceding (related) sentences. Specifically, we quantify the responsiveness of the probes to the presence of (negated) supporting and contradicting sentences, and score the probes on their consistency. We also perform a causal intervention experiment, investigating whether moving the representation of a premise along these belief directions influences the position of the hypothesis along that same direction. We find that the probes we test are generally context sensitive, but that contexts which should not affect the truth often still impact the probe outputs. Our experiments show that the type of errors depend on the layer, the (type of) model, and the kind of data. Finally, our results suggest that belief directions are (one of the) causal mediators in the inference process that incorporates in-context information.

papers.title: No Answer Needed: Predicting LLM Answer Accuracy from Question-Only Linear Probes
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) anticipate when they will answer correctly?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that a simple linear probe on residual stream activations can predict an LLM's forthcoming answer correctness, revealing a linearly separable 'factual correctness' signal that generalizes across knowledge domains but fails for mathematical reasoning.
