The interchange intervention methodology is not yet formally grounded.
The analysis only considered one location for interventions and may not capture all causal dynamics.
papers.abstract:
We address whether neural models for Natural Language Inference (NLI) can
learn the compositional interactions between lexical entailment and negation,
using four methods: the behavioral evaluation methods of (1) challenge test
sets and (2) systematic generalization tasks, and the structural evaluation
methods of (3) probes and (4) interventions. To facilitate this holistic
evaluation, we present Monotonicity NLI (MoNLI), a new naturalistic dataset
focused on lexical entailment and negation. In our behavioral evaluations, we
find that models trained on general-purpose NLI datasets fail systematically on
MoNLI examples containing negation, but that MoNLI fine-tuning addresses this
failure. In our structural evaluations, we look for evidence that our
top-performing BERT-based model has learned to implement the monotonicity
algorithm behind MoNLI. Probes yield evidence consistent with this conclusion,
and our intervention experiments bolster this, showing that the causal dynamics
of the model mirror the causal dynamics of this algorithm on subsets of MoNLI.
This suggests that the BERT model at least partially embeds a theory of lexical
entailment and negation at an algorithmic level.

papers.title: Internal Consistency and Self-Feedback in Large Language Models: A Survey
papers.core_contribution: This survey provides a unified perspective on internal consistency in LLMs, introducing the Self-Feedback framework to categorize methods for improving reasoning and reducing hallucinations.
papers.conclusion: The survey concludes that internal consistency is a key challenge in LLMs and that Self-Feedback methods are promising for improving consistency, but more research is needed.
papers.key_findings:
Internal consistency can be viewed at three levels: response, decoding, and latent, and follows an hourglass evolution pattern.
Self-Feedback, consisting of Self-Evaluation and Self-Update, is an effective framework for mining internal consistency.
The survey categorizes existing methods into lines of work for reasoning elevation and hallucination alleviation.
The paper proposes the 'Consistency Is (Almost) Correctness' hypothesis and 'The Paradox of Latent and Explicit Reasoning'.
The survey addresses the question 'Does Self-Feedback Really Work?' with an in-depth analysis.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit deficient reasoning or generate hallucinations. To address these, studies prefixed with "Self-" such as Self-Consistency, Self-Improve, and Self-Refine have been initiated. They share a commonality: involving LLMs evaluating and updating themselves. Nonetheless, these efforts lack a unified perspective on summarization, as existing surveys predominantly focus on categorization. In this paper, we use a unified perspective of internal consistency, offering explanations for reasoning deficiencies and hallucinations. Internal consistency refers to the consistency in expressions among LLMs' latent, decoding, or response layers based on sampling methodologies. Then, we introduce an effective theoretical framework capable of mining internal consistency, named Self-Feedback. This framework consists of two modules: Self-Evaluation and Self-Update. The former captures internal consistency signals, while the latter leverages the signals to enhance either the model's response or the model itself. This framework has been employed in numerous studies. We systematically classify these studies by tasks and lines of work; summarize relevant evaluation methods and benchmarks; and delve into the concern, "Does Self-Feedback Really Work?" We also propose several critical viewpoints, including the "Hourglass Evolution of Internal Consistency", "Consistency Is (Almost) Correctness" hypothesis, and "The Paradox of Latent and Explicit Reasoning". The relevant resources are open-sourced at https://github.com/IAAR-Shanghai/ICSFSurvey.

papers.title: What does the Knowledge Neuron Thesis Have to do with Knowledge?
papers.research_question: Does the Knowledge Neuron Thesis adequately explain the process of factual expression in language models?
papers.core_contribution: The Knowledge Neuron Thesis is an oversimplification; MLP weights store complex token expression patterns that are linguistically interpretable but do not constitute 'knowledge'.
papers.conclusion: The Knowledge Neuron Thesis is an oversimplification; MLP neurons store interpretable token expression patterns, not knowledge. A better understanding requires examining the entire transformer circuit, including attention mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Syntactic phenomena can be localized to specific neurons using the same gradient-based methods as factual knowledge.
Editing these identified neurons has limited impact on categorical predictions and is influenced by superficial cues like word co-occurrence frequencies.
The ROME model-editing method only superficially alters token association patterns and fails under newly proposed symmetry and synonymy criteria.
The distribution of knowledge neurons for syntactic and factual information is similar, with both occupying the topmost layers of the model.
MLP modules do not store knowledge but rather complex token expression patterns that can be interpreted linguistically.
papers.limitation:
Editing identified knowledge neurons has low reliability and is not strong enough to overturn categorical predictions.
Current circuit identification methods are ad hoc and have only been applied to a small set of tasks.
future_direction: Formalize the circuit interpretation framework and apply it to more tasks and phenomena.
Investigate the entire decision-making circuit beyond MLP modules.
papers.abstract: We reassess the Knowledge Neuron (KN) Thesis: an interpretation of the mechanism underlying the ability of large language models to recall facts from a training corpus. This nascent thesis proposes that facts are recalled from the training corpus through the MLP weights in a manner resembling key-value memory, implying in effect that "knowledge" is stored in the network. Furthermore, by modifying the MLP modules, one can control the language model's generation of factual information. The plausibility of the KN thesis has been demonstrated by the success of KN-inspired model editing methods (Dai et al., 2022; Meng et al., 2022). We find that this thesis is, at best, an oversimplification. Not only have we found that we can edit the expression of certain linguistic phenomena using the same model editing methods but, through a more comprehensive evaluation, we have found that the KN thesis does not adequately explain the process of factual expression. While it is possible to argue that the MLP weights store complex patterns that are interpretable both syntactically and semantically, these patterns do not constitute "knowledge." To gain a more comprehensive understanding of the knowledge representation process, we must look beyond the MLP weights and explore recent models' complex layer structures and attention mechanisms.

papers.title: Language Models Understand Us, Poorly
papers.research_question: What does it mean for language models to understand human language, and do current and future models achieve such understanding?
papers.core_contribution: Argues that internal representations are sufficient for language understanding, critiques the Scaling Paradigm, and advocates for probing model internals to advance the science of understanding.
papers.conclusion: Current language models have limited understanding due to under-specified data, and scaling alone may not suffice without focusing on internal representations.
papers.key_findings:
Understanding-as-representation is sufficient for language understanding, while as-reliability is necessary but not sufficient.
Current language models are limited by under-specification of meaning in their training data.
The Scaling Paradigm may be computationally infeasible for achieving human-like understanding.
Probing model internals is essential to advance the science of understanding.
Adding more modalities and human language aspects is needed for better models.
papers.limitation: The paper presents only one perspective and may not fully cover diverse fields or be ultimately correct.
future_direction: Probe model internals
Add more of human language such as intersubjective, multi-agent environments
Measure what models can learn
papers.abstract: Some claim language models understand us. Others won’t hear it. To clarify, I investigate three views of human language understanding: as-mapping, as-reliability and as-representation. I argue that while behavioral reliability is necessary for understanding, internal representations are sufficient; they climb the right hill. I review state-of-the-art language and multi-modal models: they are pragmatically challenged by under-specification of form. I question the Scaling Paradigm: limits on resources may prohibit scaled-up models from approaching understanding. Last, I describe how as-representation advances a science of understanding. We need work which probes model internals, adds more of human language, and measures what models can learn.

papers.title: Emergent World Beliefs: Exploring Transformers in Stochastic Games
papers.research_question: Do transformers learn internal world models in games of incomplete information, and how do they represent deterministic and stochastic features?
papers.core_contribution: A GPT-2 model trained on poker hand history data learns internal representations of both deterministic game structure (hand rank) and stochastic features (equity), suggesting transformers can learn belief states in partially observable environments.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can develop internal world models for games of incomplete information, learning both deterministic and stochastic features without explicit instruction.
papers.key_findings:
The model learns deterministic hand-rank representations with high accuracy (98% with MLP probe).
The model learns stochastic equity representations with a correlation coefficient of 0.59.
These representations are strongest in early layers and diminish in later layers, consistent with information bottleneck compression.
Visualization (PCA, t-SNE, UMAP) shows activation clusters corresponding to hand ranks and conceptual similarity.
The model's internal representations align with theoretical belief states in partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs).
papers.limitation:
Dataset size is limited and computationally expensive to generate, impacting model accuracy and probe results.
The synthetic data generation process may be overly simplified compared to real poker interactions.
Lack of additional datasets for validation.
No guarantee that results extend to other stochastic variables or novel domains.
future_direction: Scale the base language model.
Formalize intuitions of LLM Bayesian behavior and extract LLM beliefs of the Poker POMDP.
Use sparse autoencoders (SAEs) and further probing experiments to understand the structure of LLM predictive world representations.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong reasoning abilities across diverse fields, from solving programming challenges to competing in strategy-intensive games such as chess. Prior work has shown that LLMs can develop emergent world models in games of perfect information, where internal representations correspond to latent states of the environment. In this paper, we extend this line of investigation to domains of incomplete information, focusing on poker as a canonical partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP). We pretrain a GPT-style model on Poker Hand History (PHH) data and probe its internal activations. Our results demonstrate that the model learns both deterministic structure, such as hand ranks, and stochastic features, such as equity, without explicit instruction. Furthermore, by using primarily nonlinear probes, we demonstrated that these representations are decodeable and correlate with theoretical belief states, suggesting that LLMs are learning their own representation of the stochastic environment of Texas Hold'em Poker.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Interpretation of Multi-Step Reasoning Capabilities of Language Models
papers.research_question: Do language models perform multi-step reasoning tasks by using a reasoning mechanism or by memorizing answers from pretraining?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MechanisticProbe, a probing method that recovers reasoning trees from attention patterns, providing evidence that LMs perform multi-step reasoning mechanistically.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that reasoning trees can often be detected from LM attention patterns, supporting the claim that LMs may reason mechanistically.
papers.key_findings:
MechanisticProbe can recover reasoning trees from attention patterns of GPT-2 and LLaMA for most examples.
LMs identify useful statements in bottom layers and perform reasoning steps in higher layers.
Pruning attention heads that contribute to reasoning tree detection degrades performance, indicating a causal role.
Higher probing scores correlate with higher model accuracy and robustness to noise.
Finetuned models show clearer reasoning patterns in attention than few-shot models.
papers.limitation:
The study considered fairly simple reasoning tasks.
The analysis averages over attention heads, but heads may have different functions, especially in shallow models.
The analysis is limited to single-token prediction tasks and does not cover chain-of-thought reasoning.
future_direction: Explore more challenging reasoning tasks.
Analyze reasoning in chain-of-thought prompting settings.
papers.abstract: Yifan Hou, Jiaoda Li, Yu Fei, Alessandro Stolfo, Wangchunshu Zhou, Guangtao Zeng, Antoine Bosselut, Mrinmaya Sachan. Proceedings of the 2023 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing. 2023.

papers.title: Can LLMs Predict Their Own Failures? Self-Awareness via Internal Circuits
papers.research_question: Can LLMs predict their own failures by inspecting internal states during inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Gnosis, a lightweight self-awareness mechanism that enables frozen LLMs to perform intrinsic self-verification by decoding signals from hidden states and attention patterns with negligible inference overhead.
papers.conclusion: Gnosis provides a highly efficient framework for self-evaluation and sibling modeling, enabling early error detection and compute-aware control, demonstrating that intrinsic self-verification is both scalable and cost-effective.
papers.key_findings:
Gnosis consistently outperforms strong internal baselines and large external judges (e.g., 8B reward models, Gemini 2.5 Pro) in accuracy and calibration across math reasoning, QA, and academic knowledge benchmarks.
Gnosis generalizes zero-shot to partial generations, enabling early detection of failing trajectories and compute-aware control.
A Gnosis head trained on a small backbone transfers effectively to judge larger sibling models without fine-tuning.
Gnosis adds only ~5M parameters and operates with negligible inference cost, independent of sequence length.
Results show that reliable correctness cues are intrinsic to the generation process and can be extracted efficiently without external supervision.
papers.limitation: Gnosis is designed as a self-awareness mechanism rather than a general-purpose reward model; it transfers robustly to siblings but is not capable of acting as a general reward model.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) generate fluent and complex outputs but often fail to recognize their own mistakes and hallucinations. Existing approaches typically rely on external judges, multi-sample consistency, or text-based self-critique, which incur additional compute or correlate weakly with true correctness. We ask: can LLMs predict their own failures by inspecting internal states during inference? We introduce Gnosis, a lightweight self-awareness mechanism that enables frozen LLMs to perform intrinsic self-verification by decoding signals from hidden states and attention patterns. Gnosis passively observes internal traces, compresses them into fixed-budget descriptors, and predicts correctness with negligible inference cost, adding only ~5M parameters and operating independently of sequence length. Across math reasoning, open-domain question answering, and academic knowledge benchmarks, and over frozen backbones ranging from 1.7B to 20B parameters, Gnosis consistently outperforms strong internal baselines and large external judges in both accuracy and calibration. Moreover, it generalizes zero-shot to partial generations, enabling early detection of failing trajectories and compute-aware control. These results show that reliable correctness cues are intrinsic to generation process and can be extracted efficiently without external supervision.

papers.title: Uncovering Constraint-Based Behavior in Neural Models via Targeted\n Fine-Tuning
papers.research_question: Does competition between linguistic constraints obscure underlying linguistic knowledge in language models, and can targeted fine-tuning re-weight constraints to uncover such knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Models need to learn both linguistic constraints and their relative ranking; targeted fine-tuning can re-weight constraints to uncover dormant linguistic knowledge.
papers.conclusion: Mismatches between model and human linguistic behavior arise from either failure to learn constraints or failure to learn their ranking; targeted fine-tuning can help understand and adjust constraint rankings.
papers.key_findings:
English and Chinese models show an implicit causality (IC) bias, but Spanish and Italian models do not, due to competition with the pro-drop constraint.
Targeted fine-tuning demoting pro-drop in Spanish and Italian uncovers underlying IC knowledge.
Targeted fine-tuning promoting pro-drop in English and Chinese diminishes the IC bias.
Models learn linguistic constraints but may rank them incorrectly, leading to non-human-like behavior.
The failure to exhibit human-like behavior can be due to either not learning a constraint or not learning the correct constraint ranking.
future_direction: Pair behavioral analyses with representational probing to link model representations and behavior.
Explore constraint competition in different models like GPT-2.
Investigate other linguistic phenomena and constraints.
papers.abstract:
A growing body of literature has focused on detailing the linguistic
knowledge embedded in large, pretrained language models. Existing work has
shown that non-linguistic biases in models can drive model behavior away from
linguistic generalizations. We hypothesized that competing linguistic processes
within a language, rather than just non-linguistic model biases, could obscure
underlying linguistic knowledge. We tested this claim by exploring a single
phenomenon in four languages: English, Chinese, Spanish, and Italian. While
human behavior has been found to be similar across languages, we find
cross-linguistic variation in model behavior. We show that competing processes
in a language act as constraints on model behavior and demonstrate that
targeted fine-tuning can re-weight the learned constraints, uncovering
otherwise dormant linguistic knowledge in models. Our results suggest that
models need to learn both the linguistic constraints in a language and their
relative ranking, with mismatches in either producing non-human-like behavior.

papers.title: Emergence of Linear Truth Encodings in Language Models
papers.research_question: Why and how do linear truth subspaces that separate true from false statements emerge in language models during training and inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that linear truth encodings in language models can emerge from the statistical co-occurrence of true/false statements (Truth Co-occurrence Hypothesis), demonstrated through a toy transformer model and experiments.
papers.conclusion: Linear truth encodings in language models can emerge from the co-occurrence statistics of true and false statements, as demonstrated by a toy model and supported by experiments in pretrained models.
papers.key_findings:
Linear truth encoding emerges in a one-layer transformer trained on data where true/false statements co-occur (Truth Co-occurrence Hypothesis).
Training exhibits two phases: fast memorization of factual associations followed by slower development of linear truth separation.
Layer normalization is necessary for the linear separability of true and false representations.
The value matrix develops a block structure that enables sharpening of predictions for true sequences.
Experiments with Pythia-6.9B show similar two-phase dynamics in a large pretrained model.
papers.limitation:
The toy model is far simpler than natural training data, so the mechanism might not fully capture real-world complexity.
In real LMs, additional mechanisms likely contribute to truth encoding.
future_direction: Systematic study of mechanisms for truth encoding in real LMs.
Generalization of truth encoding across different relations.
papers.abstract: Recent probing studies reveal that large language models exhibit linear subspaces that separate true from false statements, yet the mechanism behind their emergence is unclear. We introduce a transparent, one-layer transformer toy model that reproduces such truth subspaces end-to-end and exposes one concrete route by which they can arise. We study one simple setting in which truth encoding can emerge: a data distribution where factual statements co-occur with other factual statements (and vice-versa), encouraging the model to learn this distinction in order to lower the LM loss on future tokens. We corroborate this pattern with experiments in pretrained language models. Finally, in the toy setting we observe a two-phase learning dynamic: networks first memorize individual factual associations in a few steps, then -- over a longer horizon -- learn to linearly separate true from false, which in turn lowers language-modeling loss. Together, these results provide both a mechanistic demonstration and an empirical motivation for how and why linear truth representations can emerge in language models.

papers.title: Plausibility Processing in Transformer Language Models: Focusing on the Role of Attention Heads in GPT
papers.research_question: How do Transformer language models process semantic knowledge, specifically the plausibility of noun-verb relations, and what is the causal role of attention heads in this processing?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that GPT2 processes noun-verb plausibility similarly to humans and identifies a set of attention heads that detect plausibility. It shows these heads collectively and causally contribute to the model's plausibility processing, with contributions being imbalanced and not strictly correlated with individual head performance.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that semantic plausibility knowledge in GPT2 is processed by a diffusely distributed set of attention heads that make imbalanced but collective causal contributions, highlighting the importance of causal analysis in understanding attention head functions.
papers.key_findings:
GPT2 exhibits a higher degree of similarity with humans in plausibility processing compared to other Transformer models (BERT, RoBERTa, ALBERT).
GPT2 contains 18 attention heads distributed across layers that are sensitive to noun-verb plausibility, independent of syntactic dependency.
Pruning these plausibility-processing heads eliminates GPT2's plausibility sensitivity, while pruning a random set of heads does not.
The causal contribution of individual plausibility-processing heads to the model's overall ability is imbalanced; a single head (0,10) accounts for a large portion of the effect for syntactic dependents.
The performance of an attention head in detecting plausibility (accuracy) does not necessarily correlate with its causal contribution to the model's overall plausibility processing ability.
papers.limitation:
The scope of the study is restricted to the plausibility of noun-verb relations, not covering other types of semantic knowledge.
The study does not detail how attention heads interact with other components like hidden states across layers or feed-forward networks.
future_direction: Expand the study's scope to a broader array of semantic knowledge for better generalizability.
Investigate interactions between attention heads and other model components (e.g., hidden states, feed-forward networks) to better understand their role in semantic knowledge processing.
papers.abstract: The goal of this paper is to explore how Transformer language models process semantic knowledge, especially regarding the plausibility of noun-verb relations. First, I demonstrate GPT2 exhibits a higher degree of similarity with humans in plausibility processing compared to other Transformer language models. Next, I delve into how knowledge of plausibility is contained within attention heads of GPT2 and how these heads causally contribute to GPT2's plausibility processing ability. Through several experiments, it was found that: i) GPT2 has a number of attention heads that detect plausible noun-verb relationships; ii) these heads collectively contribute to the Transformer's ability to process plausibility, albeit to varying degrees; and iii) attention heads' individual performance in detecting plausibility does not necessarily correlate with how much they contribute to GPT2's plausibility processing ability.

papers.title: A Modular Dataset to Demonstrate LLM Abstraction Capability
papers.research_question: Do LLMs have an internal representation of reasoning correctness and abstraction in reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs internally encode representations of reasoning correctness, with strongest signals in middle-late layers, and they distinguish between logical and semantic equivalence in abstract reasoning concepts.
papers.conclusion: LLMs possess internal representations of reasoning correctness and abstraction, which can inform future efforts to enhance model reliability, interpretability, and trustworthiness.
papers.key_findings:
A classifier trained on LLM activations achieves over 80% accuracy in predicting reasoning step correctness.
LLMs have internal representations of reasoning correctness, strongest in middle-late Transformer layers.
LLMs encode abstract reasoning concepts that separate logical from semantic equivalence.
Abstraction level varies across layers, with middle layers containing more abstract information.
The reasoning representations are similar across top-performing layers, suggesting redundant encoding.
papers.limitation:
Analysis restricted to structured logic puzzles, may not generalize to real-world scenarios.
Classifier's success may not generalize to other types of reasoning problems.
Reliance on probing techniques does not provide mechanistic explanation of how representations emerge.
Classifier trained on single LLM architecture, generalizability across models unclear.
future_direction: Explore more diverse reasoning benchmarks.
Conduct broader cross-model analyses including LRM models.
Develop methods for directly steering LLM reasoning based on learned representations.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit impressive capabilities but struggle with reasoning errors due to hallucinations and flawed logic. To investigate their internal representations of reasoning, we introduce ArrangementPuzzle, a novel puzzle dataset with structured solutions and automated stepwise correctness verification. We trained a classifier model on LLM activations on this dataset and found that it achieved over 80% accuracy in predicting reasoning correctness, implying that LLMs internally distinguish between correct and incorrect reasoning steps, with the strongest representations in middle-late Transformer layers. Further analysis reveals that LLMs encode abstract reasoning concepts within the middle activation layers of the transformer architecture, distinguishing logical from semantic equivalence. These findings provide insights into LLM reasoning mechanisms and contribute to improving AI reliability and interpretability, thereby offering the possibility to manipulate and refine LLM reasoning.

papers.title: Representation in large language models
papers.research_question: Is LLM behavior driven partly by representation-based information processing of the sort implicated in biological cognition, or is it driven entirely by processes of memorization and stochastic table look-up?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that LLM behavior is partially driven by representation-based information processing, contrary to the look-up table view, and outlines how mechanistic interpretability methods can be used to study these representations.
papers.conclusion: LLMs do use representation-based information processing, and we can investigate these representations using mechanistic interpretability methods.
papers.key_findings:
The look-up table view of LLMs is inadequate because it cannot explain robust behavior.
Representations, as defined by four conditions (INFORMATION, EXPLOITABILITY, BEHAVIOR, ROLE), can explain robust behavior.
Mechanistic interpretability methods like probing and causal interventions can test for representations in LLMs.
papers.abstract: The extraordinary success of recent Large Language Models (LLMs) on a diverse array of tasks has led to an explosion of scientific and philosophical theorizing aimed at explaining how they do what they do. Unfortunately, disagreement over fundamental theoretical issues has led to stalemate, with entrenched camps of LLM optimists and pessimists often committed to very different views of how these systems work. Overcoming stalemate requires agreement on fundamental questions, and the goal of this paper is to address one such question, namely: is LLM behavior driven partly by representation-based information processing of the sort implicated in biological cognition, or is it driven entirely by processes of memorization and stochastic table look-up? This is a question about what kind of algorithm LLMs implement, and the answer carries serious implications for higher level questions about whether these systems have beliefs, intentions, concepts, knowledge, and understanding. I argue that LLM behavior is partially driven by representation-based information processing, and then I describe and defend a series of practical techniques for investigating these representations and developing explanations on their basis. The resulting account provides a groundwork for future theorizing about language models and their successors.

papers.title: Exploring Concept Depth: How Large Language Models Acquire Knowledge and Concept at Different Layers?
papers.research_question: Can shallow layers in LLMs capture meaningful features of simple knowledge, while complex concepts need deeper layers to capture their meaningful features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concept of 'Concept Depth' to measure how different layers in LLMs capture concepts of varying complexity, showing that simpler concepts are learned in shallow layers while complex concepts require deeper layers.
papers.conclusion: The Concept Depth metric provides a useful framework for understanding how LLMs process concepts of varying complexity across layers, and the experimental insights enhance the understanding of internal representations in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Simpler concepts (e.g., factual knowledge) are learned in shallow layers, while more complex concepts (e.g., reasoning tasks) require deeper layers for accurate understanding.
The pattern of Concept Depth is consistent across different model families (Gemma, LLaMA, Qwen) and model sizes.
Larger models within a family tend to achieve higher peak accuracy and sometimes converge to optimal performance at earlier layers.
Adding noise to the input or quantizing model weights (e.g., to 8-bit) slows down the convergence of concept understanding, requiring deeper layers to achieve comparable accuracy.
Compressing models to 16-bit quantization does not significantly harm the understanding process compared to 32-bit.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable performances across a wide range of tasks. However, the mechanisms by which these models encode tasks of varying complexities remain poorly understood. In this paper, we explore the hypothesis that LLMs process concepts of varying complexities in different layers, introducing the idea of "Concept Depth" to suggest that more complex concepts are typically acquired in deeper layers. Specifically, we categorize concepts based on their level of abstraction, defining them in the order of increasing complexity within factual, emotional, and inferential tasks. We conduct extensive probing experiments using layer-wise representations across various LLM families (Gemma, LLaMA, Qwen) on various datasets spanning the three domains of tasks. Our findings reveal that models could efficiently conduct probing for simpler tasks in shallow layers, and more complex tasks typically necessitate deeper layers for accurate understanding. Additionally, we examine how external factors, such as adding noise to the input and quantizing the model weights, might affect layer-wise representations. Our findings suggest that these factors can impede the development of a conceptual understanding of LLMs until deeper layers are explored. We hope that our proposed concept and experimental insights will enhance the understanding of the mechanisms underlying LLMs. Our codes are available at https://github.com/Luckfort/CD.

papers.title: Structured World Representations in Maze-Solving Transformers
papers.research_question: How do transformers learn to solve mazes and what internal representations do they form?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers trained on maze-solving tasks learn linear representations of maze connectivity in their residual stream, and specific attention heads (adjacency heads) handle path-following by attending to valid neighbors.
papers.conclusion: Transformers acquire emergent linear representations of maze connectivity encoded in a single token's latent state, and their embedding layers learn spatial structure; specific attention heads are identified that respect maze topology.
papers.key_findings:
The residual stream of a single token (e.g., <PATH_START>) can be linearly decoded to reconstruct the entire maze structure.
The embedding layer learns an emergent spatial structure where distances between coordinate tokens correlate with Manhattan distances on the grid.
Specific attention heads (e.g., Layer 5, Head 3) consistently attend to tokens at path length 1 from the current position, acting as adjacency heads that respect maze topology.
The formation of linearly decodable maze representations coincides with grokking-like transitions where generalization performance improves sharply.
Models often violate maze constraints (e.g., pass through walls) but still reach the target, indicating imperfect learning of constraints.
papers.limitation:
The generalizability of findings from toy models to larger scales remains uncertain.
Models often violate maze constraints (e.g., pass through walls) even when reaching the target.
future_direction: Construct a more complete mechanistic picture of how elementary heads operate over the linear world model to form circuits for solving mazes.
Investigate the generality of emergent models by training different neural network architectures on the same tasks with different input representations.
papers.abstract: Transformer models underpin many recent advances in practical machine learning applications, yet understanding their internal behavior continues to elude researchers. Given the size and complexity of these models, forming a comprehensive picture of their inner workings remains a significant challenge. To this end, we set out to understand small transformer models in a more tractable setting: that of solving mazes. In this work, we focus on the abstractions formed by these models and find evidence for the consistent emergence of structured internal representations of maze topology and valid paths. We demonstrate this by showing that the residual stream of only a single token can be linearly decoded to faithfully reconstruct the entire maze. We also find that the learned embeddings of individual tokens have spatial structure. Furthermore, we take steps towards deciphering the circuity of path-following by identifying attention heads (dubbed $\textit{adjacency heads}$), which are implicated in finding valid subsequent tokens.

papers.title: Loop as a Bridge: Can Looped Transformers Truly Link Representation Space and Natural Language Outputs?
papers.research_question: Can Looped Transformers align linguistic verification output with representations? Can LTs enhance their introspective awareness on representations?
papers.core_contribution: Increasing loop iterations in Looped Transformers narrows the gap between self-verification and representation readout, but partly due to degradation of representation quality. Moreover, LTs only show introspective awareness in the final loop, not continuously across loops.
papers.conclusion: Current Looped Transformers do not yet achieve continuous introspection across loops, and the observed gap narrowing is partly driven by a degradation in representation quality.
papers.key_findings:
The accuracy of textual self-verification improves with more loop iterations.
The performance of representation-based linear probes declines with more loop iterations.
The gap between representation readout and self-verification narrows with more loops, but partly because of the decline in representation readout.
LTs are only aware of injected concepts when the injection occurs in the final loop, not in earlier loops.
papers.limitation: The experiments are a preliminary exploration conducted on a single specific implementation of LTs (Ouro), so the observed limitations should not be interpreted as intrinsic flaws of the general LTs paradigm.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often exhibit a gap between their internal knowledge and their explicit linguistic outputs. In this report, we empirically investigate whether Looped Transformers (LTs)--architectures that increase computational depth by iterating shared layers--can bridge this gap by utilizing their iterative nature as a form of introspection. Our experiments reveal that while increasing loop iterations narrows the gap, it is partly driven by a degradation of their internal knowledge carried by representations. Moreover, another empirical analysis suggests that current LTs' ability to perceive representations does not improve across loops; it is only present in the final loop. These results suggest that while LTs offer a promising direction for scaling computational depth, they have yet to achieve the introspection required to truly link representation space and natural language.

papers.title: Sparse Neurons Carry Strong Signals of Question Ambiguity in LLMs
papers.research_question: How is question ambiguity encoded in the internal representations of LLMs, and can it be detected and controlled at the neuron level?
papers.core_contribution: Question ambiguity is sparsely encoded in a small set of neurons (AENs) in LLMs, and steering these neurons can control the model's behavior from answering to abstention.
papers.conclusion: Ambiguity is encoded in a compact, model-specific subspace of neurons, enabling interpretable and controllable behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Ambiguity is linearly encoded in LLM internal representations and can be detected with high accuracy using linear probes.
A small set of neurons (AENs) encode ambiguity, with as few as one neuron being sufficient.
Probes trained only on AENs achieve strong performance and generalize across datasets.
Activation steering on AENs causally shifts model behavior from direct answering to abstention.
AENs emerge in shallow layers and capture a large proportion of the full steering effect.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to three instruction-tuned LLMs and two datasets, and broader validation is needed.
future_direction: Extend analysis to the token level to see how ambiguity arises within a question and influences model uncertainty.
papers.abstract: Ambiguity is pervasive in real-world questions, yet large language models (LLMs) often respond with confident answers rather than seeking clarification. In this work, we show that question ambiguity is linearly encoded in the internal representations of LLMs and can be both detected and controlled at the neuron level. During the model's pre-filling stage, we identify that a small number of neurons, as few as one, encode question ambiguity information. Probes trained on these Ambiguity-Encoding Neurons (AENs) achieve strong performance on ambiguity detection and generalize across datasets, outperforming prompting-based and representation-based baselines. Layerwise analysis reveals that AENs emerge from shallow layers, suggesting early encoding of ambiguity signals in the model's processing pipeline. Finally, we show that through manipulating AENs, we can control LLM's behavior from direct answering to abstention. Our findings reveal that LLMs form compact internal representations of question ambiguity, enabling interpretable and controllable behavior.

papers.title: Representation Engineering for Large-Language Models: Survey and Research Challenges
papers.research_question: This paper investigates the goals, methods, and challenges of representation engineering as an approach to make large-language models more predictable and controllable.
papers.core_contribution: This paper formalizes the goals and methods of representation engineering, providing a cohesive survey of this emerging discipline and outlining a research agenda for building more predictable and controllable large-language models.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that representation engineering is a promising approach for enhancing LLM transparency and control, and it provides a clear agenda for future research to address current challenges.
papers.key_findings:
Representation engineering uses contrasting inputs to detect and edit high-level representations, offering a top-down approach to model interpretability and control.
It compares favorably with alternative approaches like mechanistic interpretability and prompt-engineering in certain aspects.
Risks include performance degradation, increased compute time, and steerability issues.
The linear representation hypothesis underpins representation engineering, but its strong form may not hold, limiting generalizability.
Future research should focus on dynamic, safe, and personalizable LLMs through representation engineering.
papers.limitation:
Performance decrease, compute time increases, and steerability issues.
The strong linear representation hypothesis may not hold, limiting generalized interventions.
future_direction: Build predictable, dynamic, safe, and personalizable LLMs through representation engineering.
papers.abstract: Large-language models are capable of completing a variety of tasks, but remain unpredictable and intractable. Representation engineering seeks to resolve this problem through a new approach utilizing samples of contrasting inputs to detect and edit high-level representations of concepts such as honesty, harmfulness or power-seeking. We formalize the goals and methods of representation engineering to present a cohesive picture of work in this emerging discipline. We compare it with alternative approaches, such as mechanistic interpretability, prompt-engineering and fine-tuning. We outline risks such as performance decrease, compute time increases and steerability issues. We present a clear agenda for future research to build predictable, dynamic, safe and personalizable LLMs.

papers.title: Layer by Layer: Uncovering Hidden Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: Does the final layer always yield the best representation for downstream tasks, or can intermediate layers provide better representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that intermediate layers in language models often outperform final layers on downstream tasks, and introduces a unified information-theoretic framework to explain this phenomenon.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that intermediate layers often provide superior representations, challenging the default use of final layers, and provides a framework for understanding representation quality.
papers.key_findings:
Intermediate layers consistently outperform final layers across diverse architectures and tasks.
Autoregressive models exhibit a pronounced mid-layer compression valley, while masked or bidirectional models show milder changes.
The effect is domain-general, also observed in autoregressive vision transformers.
Chain-of-thought fine-tuning reshapes mid-layer entropy, preserving latent context for multi-step reasoning.
Intermediate layers strike a balance between information compression and signal preservation.
future_direction: Investigate the underlying causes of intermediate layer compression and do explicit finetuning to control compression.
papers.abstract: From extracting features to generating text, the outputs of large language models (LLMs) typically rely on the final layers, following the conventional wisdom that earlier layers capture only low-level cues. However, our analysis shows that intermediate layers can encode even richer representations, often improving performance on a range of downstream tasks. To explain and quantify these hidden-layer properties, we propose a unified framework of representation quality metrics based on information theory, geometry, and invariance to input perturbations. Our framework highlights how each layer balances information compression and signal preservation, revealing why mid-depth embeddings can exceed the last layer's performance. Through extensive experiments on 32 text-embedding tasks across various architectures (transformers, state-space models) and domains (language, vision), we demonstrate that intermediate layers consistently provide stronger features, challenging the standard view on final-layer embeddings and opening new directions on using mid-layer representations for more robust and accurate representations.

papers.title: The Compositional Architecture of Regret in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Which transformer layers’ hidden states most cleanly isolate the regret signal, and how is this signal represented with these layers?
papers.core_contribution: This work contributes valuable insights for neuron-level identification and provides methodological tools for analyzing similar cognitive states, advancing our understanding of how cognitive states are coded within LLMs.
papers.conclusion: This work advances our understanding of how cognitive states like regret are coded within LLMs through neuron-level identification and analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Identified the optimal regret representation layer using the S-CDI metric, enhancing probe classification performance.
Discovered an M-shaped decoupling pattern across transformer layers, indicating alternating coupling and decoupling phases in information processing.
Categorized neurons into three functional groups (regret, non-regret, dual) using the RDS metric.
Showed that simultaneous intervention with regret and dual neurons substantially reduces regret classification performance, revealing a compositional architecture of regret at the neuron level.
Revealed that regret processing capabilities exhibit non-monotonic scaling across model sizes, with the 70B model showing superior performance.
papers.limitation: The non-monotonic scaling observed lacks more detailed investigation.
future_direction: Validation of the two-factor performance hypothesis in future work.
papers.abstract: Regret in Large Language Models refers to their explicit regret expression when presented with evidence contradicting their previously generated misinformation. Studying the regret mechanism is crucial for enhancing model reliability and helps in revealing how cognition is coded in neural networks. To understand this mechanism, we need to first identify regret expressions in model outputs, then analyze their internal representation. This analysis requires examining the model's hidden states, where information processing occurs at the neuron level. However, this faces three key challenges: (1) the absence of specialized datasets capturing regret expressions, (2) the lack of metrics to find the optimal regret representation layer, and (3) the lack of metrics for identifying and analyzing regret neurons. Addressing these limitations, we propose: (1) a workflow for constructing a comprehensive regret dataset through strategically designed prompting scenarios, (2) the Supervised Compression-Decoupling Index (S-CDI) metric to identify optimal regret representation layers, and (3) the Regret Dominance Score (RDS) metric to identify regret neurons and the Group Impact Coefficient (GIC) to analyze activation patterns. Our experimental results successfully identified the optimal regret representation layer using the S-CDI metric, which significantly enhanced performance in probe classification experiments. Additionally, we discovered an M-shaped decoupling pattern across model layers, revealing how information processing alternates between coupling and decoupling phases. Through the RDS metric, we categorized neurons into three distinct functional groups: regret neurons, non-regret neurons, and dual neurons.

papers.title: Mechanistic Evidence for Faithfulness Decay in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: Does chain-of-thought reasoning reflect the model's actual decision-making process, or is it merely post-hoc justification?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces NLDD, a metric for step-level faithfulness in chain-of-thought reasoning, and discovers a consistent Reasoning Horizon (k*) at 70–85% of chain length beyond which reasoning tokens have little or negative effect on the final answer.
papers.conclusion: NLDD quantifies the causal influence of reasoning chains on model predictions, revealing that high accuracy can mask a lack of causal dependence on CoT, and identifies a reasoning horizon beyond which steps contribute minimally or negatively.
papers.key_findings:
Different architectures exhibit distinct faithfulness patterns (faithful vs. anti-faithful regimes).
The Mapping Gap demonstrates models can encode task-relevant structure in internal representations without utilizing it for prediction.
The reasoning horizon (k*) is a consistent transition point at 70-85% of chain length where causal influence decays.
NLDD reveals failure modes that accuracy-based evaluation misses, such as anti-faithful behavior.
For anti-faithful models, extended reasoning beyond the horizon can be harmful, acting as a causal distractor.
papers.limitation:
Truncates chains rather than replacing corrupted steps, which conflates weak reliance on a step with sufficiency of prior steps.
Logit normalization assumes architectural differences affect margins and variance proportionally, which is empirically supported but not guaranteed.
TAS and RSA analysis uses a single middle layer; layer-wise variation is small but comprehensive analysis may reveal depth-dependent effects.
Evaluation is limited to three tasks (100 samples each), two of which are synthetic, and to decoder-only models.
Uses greedy decoding with fixed prompts; stochastic decoding may shift horizon locations.
Step-based analysis assumes explicit chain structure; free-form CoT would require different segmentation.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) explanations are widely used to interpret how language models solve complex problems, yet it remains unclear whether these step-by-step explanations reflect how the model actually reaches its answer, or merely post-hoc justifications. We propose Normalized Logit Difference Decay (NLDD), a metric that measures whether individual reasoning steps are faithful to the model's decision-making process. Our approach corrupts individual reasoning steps from the explanation and measures how much the model's confidence in its answer drops, to determine if a step is truly important. By standardizing these measurements, NLDD enables rigorous cross-model comparison across different architectures. Testing three model families across syntactic, logical, and arithmetic tasks, we discover a consistent Reasoning Horizon (k*) at 70--85% of chain length, beyond which reasoning tokens have little or negative effect on the final answer. We also find that models can encode correct internal representations while completely failing the task. These results show that accuracy alone does not reveal whether a model actually reasons through its chain. NLDD offers a way to measure when CoT matters.

papers.title: ReFT: Representation Finetuning for Language Models
papers.research_question: Can editing representations, instead of weights, be a more powerful alternative for parameter-efficient finetuning of language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Representation Finetuning (ReFT), a family of parameter-efficient finetuning methods that edit hidden representations instead of weights, and shows that it is more parameter-efficient and often outperforms existing PEFTs.
papers.conclusion: ReFT methods are a promising alternative to weight-based PEFTs, offering a better balance of efficiency and performance, and are worthy of further exploration.
papers.key_findings:
ReFT methods are 15×–65× more parameter-efficient than LoRA.
LoReFT achieves state-of-the-art performance on commonsense reasoning, instruction-following, and natural language understanding.
ReFT methods are less effective on arithmetic reasoning tasks, possibly due to the length of chain-of-thought generations.
ReFT performance scales with model size.
LoReFT outperforms full finetuning on instruction-following with only 0.0039% of parameters.
papers.limitation: ReFTs may have trouble with chain-of-thought reasoning tasks due to the length of generations and overall greater difficulty of the task.
papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient finetuning (PEFT) methods seek to adapt large neural models via updates to a small number of weights. However, much prior interpretability work has shown that representations encode rich semantic information, suggesting that editing representations might be a more powerful alternative. We pursue this hypothesis by developing a family of Representation Finetuning (ReFT) methods. ReFT methods operate on a frozen base model and learn task-specific interventions on hidden representations. We define a strong instance of the ReFT family, Low-rank Linear Subspace ReFT (LoReFT), and we identify an ablation of this method that trades some performance for increased efficiency. Both are drop-in replacements for existing PEFTs and learn interventions that are 15x--65x more parameter-efficient than LoRA. We showcase LoReFT on eight commonsense reasoning tasks, four arithmetic reasoning tasks, instruction-tuning, and GLUE. In all these evaluations, our ReFTs deliver the best balance of efficiency and performance, and almost always outperform state-of-the-art PEFTs. We release a generic ReFT training library publicly at https://github.com/stanfordnlp/pyreft.

papers.title: Constrained belief updates explain geometric structures in transformer representations
papers.research_question: What computational structures emerge in transformers trained on next-token prediction? How do transformers resolve the conflict between optimal Bayesian belief updating (a recursive process) and their parallelized, attention-driven architecture?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that transformers implement constrained Bayesian belief updating—a parallelized version of partial Bayesian inference shaped by architectural constraints. It explains why specific intermediate geometric structures emerge in transformer representations.
papers.conclusion: The geometric structures in transformer representations are a mathematical signature of how architectural constraints warp optimal Bayesian inference, revealing a precise interplay between theoretical necessity and implementation.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers implement constrained Bayesian belief updating due to architectural constraints, bending optimal Bayesian inference into attention's parallelizable form.
The attention mechanism in the first layer implements a spectral algorithm that builds constrained beliefs, with attention weights approximating the decay of influence via eigenvalues of the data-generating transition matrix.
Intermediate representations (after attention) are fractals matching the constrained belief geometry, while final representations (after MLP) match the full, unconstrained belief geometry.
The attention pattern, OV vectors, and token embeddings can be theoretically predicted from the constrained belief updating equations.
For negative eigenvalues in the transition matrix (oscillatory dynamics), multiple attention heads are required to capture the full update pattern due to the non-negativity constraint of attention.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is conducted on a tractable family of hidden Markov models (Mess3), which is a simplified setting.
As the HMM parameter α moves away from a central range, deviations between predicted and actual representations increase, and a complete characterization of these deviations remains for future work.
future_direction: A complete characterization of how deviations between predicted and actual representations scale with the HMM parameter α.
Applying the methodology to more complex cases, such as large language models trained on natural text, where the same tension between architecture and optimal inference is anticipated.
papers.abstract: What computational structures emerge in transformers trained on next-token prediction? In this work, we provide evidence that transformers implement constrained Bayesian belief updating -- a parallelized version of partial Bayesian inference shaped by architectural constraints. We integrate the model-agnostic theory of optimal prediction with mechanistic interpretability to analyze transformers trained on a tractable family of hidden Markov models that generate rich geometric patterns in neural activations. Our primary analysis focuses on single-layer transformers, revealing how the first attention layer implements these constrained updates, with extensions to multi-layer architectures demonstrating how subsequent layers refine these representations. We find that attention carries out an algorithm with a natural interpretation in the probability simplex, and create representations with distinctive geometric structure. We show how both the algorithmic behavior and the underlying geometry of these representations can be theoretically predicted in detail -- including the attention pattern, OV-vectors, and embedding vectors -- by modifying the equations for optimal future token predictions to account for the architectural constraints of attention. Our approach provides a principled lens on how architectural constraints shape the implementation of optimal prediction, revealing why transformers develop specific intermediate geometric structures.

papers.title: Measuring Faithfulness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: Does chain-of-thought reasoning faithfully explain the model's actual reasoning process?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes tests for measuring faithfulness of chain-of-thought reasoning and finds that faithfulness varies across tasks and model sizes, with smaller models often producing more faithful reasoning.
papers.conclusion: Chain-of-thought reasoning is not always faithful, but it can be faithful under carefully chosen circumstances such as model size and task. Smaller models may be better to use if faithful reasoning is important.
papers.key_findings:
Models show large variation across tasks in how strongly they condition on the CoT when predicting their answer.
CoT's performance boost does not come from added test-time compute alone or from information encoded via the particular phrasing of the CoT.
As models become larger and more capable, they produce less faithful reasoning on most tasks studied.
Smaller models often generate more faithful reasoning than larger, more capable ones.
Faithfulness depends on model size and task difficulty, with easier tasks and larger models leading to less faithful reasoning.
papers.limitation:
Lack of ground truth about the model's internal reasoning process, making it impossible to know if CoT is truly faithful.
Analysis limited to RLHF-finetuned models; faithfulness may differ for pretrained LLMs or other training schemes.
future_direction: Investigate training schemes different from RLHF for eliciting more faithful reasoning.
Use the proposed metrics to increase the faithfulness of CoT and build systems with trustworthy reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) perform better when they produce step-by-step, "Chain-of-Thought" (CoT) reasoning before answering a question, but it is unclear if the stated reasoning is a faithful explanation of the model's actual reasoning (i.e., its process for answering the question). We investigate hypotheses for how CoT reasoning may be unfaithful, by examining how the model predictions change when we intervene on the CoT (e.g., by adding mistakes or paraphrasing it). Models show large variation across tasks in how strongly they condition on the CoT when predicting their answer, sometimes relying heavily on the CoT and other times primarily ignoring it. CoT's performance boost does not seem to come from CoT's added test-time compute alone or from information encoded via the particular phrasing of the CoT. As models become larger and more capable, they produce less faithful reasoning on most tasks we study. Overall, our results suggest that CoT can be faithful if the circumstances such as the model size and task are carefully chosen.

papers.title: Counterfactual reasoning: an analysis of in-context emergence
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether language models can perform in-context counterfactual reasoning, i.e., predicting consequences of hypothetical scenarios by inferring unobserved latent concepts and copying contextual noise from factual observations.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that language models are capable of in-context counterfactual reasoning, and through analysis of Transformers, finds that self-attention, model depth, and pre-training data diversity drive performance, with mechanistic evidence that the latent concept is linearly represented in the residual stream and that designated noise abduction heads emerge.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can perform counterfactual reasoning by leveraging self-attention and depth, and this ability extends to sequential data, suggesting potential for counterfactual story generation.
papers.key_findings:
Language models can perform in-context counterfactual reasoning on synthetic linear regression tasks.
Self-attention is crucial for counterfactual reasoning; MLP-only models fail.
Model depth improves counterfactual reasoning performance.
Pre-training data diversity improves performance and out-of-distribution generalization.
The latent parameter is linearly encoded in the residual stream, and designated noise abduction heads emerge in attention layers.
papers.limitation: The synthetic setup may not fully capture the complexity of natural language counterfactual reasoning.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to natural language tasks and more complex functions.
Further exploration of the role of attention heads in counterfactual reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large-scale neural language models exhibit remarkable performance in in-context learning: the ability to learn and reason about the input context on the fly. This work studies in-context counterfactual reasoning in language models, that is, the ability to predict consequences of a hypothetical scenario. We focus on a well-defined, synthetic linear regression task that requires noise abduction. Accurate prediction is based on (1) inferring an unobserved latent concept and (2) copying contextual noise from factual observations. We show that language models are capable of counterfactual reasoning. Further, we enhance existing identifiability results and reduce counterfactual reasoning for a broad class of functions to a transformation on in-context observations. In Transformers, we find that self-attention, model depth and pre-training data diversity drive performance. Moreover, we provide mechanistic evidence that the latent concept is linearly represented in the residual stream and we introduce designated \textit{noise abduction heads} central to performing counterfactual reasoning. Lastly, our findings extend to counterfactual reasoning under SDE dynamics and reflect that Transformers can perform noise abduction on sequential data, providing preliminary evidence on the potential for counterfactual story generation. Our code is available under https://github.com/mrtzmllr/iccr.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Emotion Inference in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do autoregressive large language models internally represent and process emotional information to infer emotions from text?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that emotion representations in LLMs are functionally localized to mid-layers and that causal interventions on appraisal concepts can steer emotion inference in psychologically plausible ways.
papers.conclusion: This work provides a mechanistic understanding of emotion inference in LLMs and demonstrates causal intervention methods to control emotion inference, with potential applications in safety and alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Emotion representations are functionally localized to specific mid-layers across diverse model families and sizes.
Activation patching reveals that MHSA and FFN units in mid-layers are critical for emotion inference.
Attention patterns in mid-layers shift to emotionally loaded tokens.
Appraisal concepts are linearly represented in the model and their modulation can steer emotion inference.
The structure of emotion representations aligns with cognitive appraisal theory from psychology.
papers.limitation: Focusing only on correctly classified examples may introduce bias toward unambiguous emotional content.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) show promising capabilities in predicting human emotions from text. However, the mechanisms through which these models process emotional stimuli remain largely unexplored. Our study addresses this gap by investigating how autoregressive LLMs infer emotions, showing that emotion representations are functionally localized to specific regions in the model. Our evaluation includes diverse model families and sizes and is supported by robustness checks. We then show that the identified representations are psychologically plausible by drawing on cognitive appraisal theory, a well-established psychological framework positing that emotions emerge from evaluations (appraisals) of environmental stimuli. By causally intervening on construed appraisal concepts, we steer the generation and show that the outputs align with theoretical and intuitive expectations. This work highlights a novel way to causally intervene and precisely shape emotional text generation, potentially benefiting safety and alignment in sensitive affective domains.

papers.title: Semantic Composition in Visually Grounded Language Models
papers.research_question: This thesis explores whether and how models compose visually grounded semantics, and how we might improve their ability to do so.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces multiple methods (WinogroundVQA, Syntactic Neural Module Distillation, Causal Tracing, Syntactic MeanPool, Cross-modal Attention Congruence Regularization) to probe, analyze, and improve the compositional abilities of visually grounded language models.
papers.conclusion: The work explores the compositionality of visually grounded semantics, introducing methods to probe and improve it, and draws connections to neuroscience, psycholinguistics, formal semantics, and philosophy.
papers.key_findings:
Generative vision-language models like BLIP 2.0 and MiniGPT-4 perform poorly on the compositional WinogroundVQA benchmark.
Syntactic Neural Module Distillation reveals that larger sentence embedding models (GTR-T5) are more compositional, but model size is not the only determining factor.
Cross-modal Attention Congruence Regularization (CACR) improves relation alignment in vision-language models and outperforms the previous state-of-the-art method (IAIS) on the Winoground benchmark.
papers.limitation:
Due to compute restrictions, hyperparameter tuning for the SynNaMoN experiments was unfeasible, and the dataset had to be constrained to a subset of trees and production rules.
The choice of linguistic formalism (Penn Treebank) may influence the probing results of compositional structure.
future_direction: Exploring whether different linguistic formalisms are better proxies for a model's compositional structure.
Further work on the causal tracing experiment for image captioning models (implementation in progress).
papers.abstract: What is sentence meaning and its ideal representation? Much of the expressive power of human language derives from semantic composition, the mind's ability to represent meaning hierarchically & relationally over constituents. At the same time, much sentential meaning is outside the text and requires grounding in sensory, motor, and experiential modalities to be adequately learned. Although large language models display considerable compositional ability, recent work shows that visually-grounded language models drastically fail to represent compositional structure. In this thesis, we explore whether & how models compose visually grounded semantics, and how we might improve their ability to do so. Specifically, we introduce 1) WinogroundVQA, a new compositional visual question answering benchmark, 2) Syntactic Neural Module Distillation, a measure of compositional ability in sentence embedding models, 3) Causal Tracing for Image Captioning Models to locate neural representations vital for vision-language composition, 4) Syntactic MeanPool to inject a compositional inductive bias into sentence embeddings, and 5) Cross-modal Attention Congruence Regularization, a self-supervised objective function for vision-language relation alignment. We close by discussing connections of our work to neuroscience, psycholinguistics, formal semantics, and philosophy.

papers.title: Using Neural Networks to Generate Inferential Roles for Natural Language
papers.research_question: How can neural networks be used to generate inferential roles for natural language, i.e., predict which sentences are likely to follow from a given sentence?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that a tree-structured neural network can be trained to generate inferential roles (entailments) for sentences, and argues for an inferentialist approach to semantics where meaning is characterized by inferential relations.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks can be used to formalize an inferentialist approach to semantics, where the meaning of a linguistic expression is characterized by the inferential roles it plays.
papers.key_findings:
The model generates plausible entailments for novel sentences, as indicated by human plausibility ratings.
Human ratings show model-generated entailments are rated positively and closer to human-generated entailments than contradictions.
The model can generate chains of entailments, building inferential networks around a sentence.
The model can interpolate between known examples to produce novel inferential transitions.
The model can be conditioned on queries to generate specific entailments, demonstrating selective navigation of inferential roles.
papers.limitation:
Generated sentences are sometimes defective (e.g., agreement errors, misplaced words) or incomprehensible.
The model does not consider the relationship between linguistic expressions and the non-linguistic world.
future_direction: Using increased amounts of training data.
Using more sophisticated network architectures (e.g., Tree LSTM, Recursive Neural Tensor Network, lifted matrix-space model).
Incorporating non-linguistic perceptions and actions to account for the relationship between language and the world.
papers.abstract: Neural networks have long been used to study linguistic phenomena spanning the domains of phonology, morphology, syntax, and semantics. Of these domains, semantics is somewhat unique in that there is little clarity concerning what a model needs to be able to do in order to provide an account of how the meanings of complex linguistic expressions, such as sentences, are understood. We argue that one thing such models need to be able to do is generate predictions about which further sentences are likely to follow from a given sentence; these define the sentence's "inferential role." We then show that it is possible to train a tree-structured neural network model to generate very simple examples of such inferential roles using the recently released Stanford Natural Language Inference (SNLI) dataset. On an empirical front, we evaluate the performance of this model by reporting entailment prediction accuracies on a set of test sentences not present in the training data. We also report the results of a simple study that compares human plausibility ratings for both human-generated and model-generated entailments for a random selection of sentences in this test set. On a more theoretical front, we argue in favor of a revision to some common assumptions about semantics: understanding a linguistic expression is not only a matter of mapping it onto a representation that somehow constitutes its meaning; rather, understanding a linguistic expression is mainly a matter of being able to draw certain inferences. Inference should accordingly be at the core of any model of semantic cognition.

papers.title: Circular Reasoning: Understanding Self-Reinforcing Loops in Large Reasoning Models
papers.research_question: What is the 'Circular Reasoning' failure mode in Large Reasoning Models, and how can we systematically analyze its mechanisms and predict its onset?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies the 'Circular Reasoning' failure mode in Large Reasoning Models, introduces LoopBench for systematic evaluation, analyzes the mechanisms (state collapse, triggers, persistence via V-shaped attention), and proposes an early prediction method using CUSUM on hidden states.
papers.conclusion: Circular reasoning is a critical failure mode in LRMs that stems from intrinsic generation mechanisms, and the proposed analysis and prediction method provide a foundation for improving reasoning stability.
papers.key_findings:
Circular reasoning manifests as two distinct loop types: numerical loops (universal) and statement loops (prevalent in reasoning models).
LoopBench triggers significantly higher repetition rates than existing benchmarks, revealing model fragility.
The loop onset is triggered by reasoning impasses and sustained by a self-reinforcing V-shaped attention pattern.
Early prediction of statement loops is feasible by monitoring hidden state shifts with the CUSUM algorithm.
Decoding strategies mitigate but do not eliminate repetition, indicating an inherent trade-off between loop and accuracy.
papers.limitation:
LoopBench focuses on specific task patterns (high-precision arithmetic and complex recursive reasoning) and may not cover all reasoning scenarios.
The early prediction method is only validated for statement loops, not numerical loops.
The analysis is primarily conducted on open-source models, limiting generalizability to closed-source models.
future_direction: Expand LoopBench to more diverse tasks and domains.
Investigate loop mitigation strategies, such as dynamic decoding or architectural modifications.
Extend the analysis to more model architectures and scales.
papers.abstract: Despite the success of test-time scaling, Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) frequently encounter repetitive loops that lead to computational waste and inference failure. In this paper, we identify a distinct failure mode termed Circular Reasoning. Unlike traditional model degeneration, this phenomenon manifests as a self-reinforcing trap where generated content acts as a logical premise for its own recurrence, compelling the reiteration of preceding text. To systematically analyze this phenomenon, we introduce LoopBench, a dataset designed to capture two distinct loop typologies: numerical loops and statement loops. Mechanistically, we characterize circular reasoning as a state collapse exhibiting distinct boundaries, where semantic repetition precedes textual repetition. We reveal that reasoning impasses trigger the loop onset, which subsequently persists as an inescapable cycle driven by a self-reinforcing V-shaped attention mechanism. Guided by these findings, we employ the Cumulative Sum (CUSUM) algorithm to capture these precursors for early loop prediction. Experiments across diverse LRMs validate its accuracy and elucidate the stability of long-chain reasoning.

papers.title: A Survey on the Honesty of Large Language Models
papers.core_contribution: This survey provides a comprehensive overview of honesty in large language models, covering its definitions, evaluation approaches, and strategies for improvement, and suggests future research directions.
papers.conclusion: The survey consolidates research on LLM honesty, highlighting the importance of self-knowledge and self-expression, and calls for further exploration to improve model trustworthiness.
papers.key_findings:
Honesty in LLMs is defined as comprising self-knowledge (recognizing known and unknown) and self-expression (faithfully expressing knowledge).
Current LLMs exhibit dishonest behaviors such as confidently presenting wrong answers or failing to express what they know.
Evaluation of honesty includes recognition of known/unknown, calibration, and selective prediction.
Improvement approaches are categorized into training-free (e.g., prompting, decoding-time intervention) and training-based (e.g., fine-tuning, reinforcement learning).
Future research directions include addressing honesty in instruction-following, in-context knowledge, and various models.
future_direction: Objective or Subjective
Knowledge Identification
Honesty in Instruction-following
Honesty on In-context Knowledge
Honesty in Various Models
papers.abstract: Honesty is a fundamental principle for aligning large language models (LLMs) with human values, requiring these models to recognize what they know and don't know and be able to faithfully express their knowledge.
